title: Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?
description:
Alongside warnings about its ability to destroy humanity, artificial intelligence is also hailed for its potential to revolutionise health treatment. Just how far can it take us?
Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.
I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window.
fullText:
Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.

I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window. With her liver failing, her skin was a ghostly apricot. June – I called her Nan – had been stalked by the king of terrors, the emperor of all maladies: cancer. That son of a bitch.

The cancer was in her pancreas. Odds of survival? “Not good” – putting it lightly. The maths, putting it darkly: it’s the 12th most common cancer worldwide, the sixth most common cause of cancer death. The World Health Organization says it is “one of the cancer types with the least favourable prognosis”. It was not favourable for my grandmother.

June died nine years ago. Lately I’ve been thinking about alternate futures – the ones in which my grandmother, and the many millions diagnosed with cancer each year, are still here. The thoughts creep in as we are bombarded by artificial intelligence chief executives making bold proclamations such as “AI will cure cancer in five to 10 years” or “AI will cure cancer in our lifetimes”. Those claims stand in contrast to apocalyptic scenarios, including AI being responsible for human extinction before 2030. AI, we hear, is both saviour and annihilator.

Park the world-ending scenarios and you’ll find there has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer. If there is a future where a supposed AI apocalypse is averted, then it may be one in which cancer therapy has been completely redefined. But just how far can AI take us towards a cure?

Today AI is being turned toward drug development, treatment plans and, in some places, it’s being used clinically, studying imagery of lungs for early signs of malignancy and helping to remove brain tumours. Words like “efficiency” and “personalised care” are everywhere; the notion AI can free up time for doctors and medical professionals to get away from the busywork abound.

Even with such positive advances, speak to clinicians, oncologists and researchers working at the coalface and you quickly find there is tension between the more grandiose claims of big tech and its race to “solve” disease, and the deliberate, considered progress of science.

“Until AI can actually think and do experiments itself at scale, I’m not sure that we’re going to find a cure for all cancer or medical illness in the next 10 years,” says Sherene Loi, a medical oncologist who specialises in breast cancer treatment at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne.

But Loi and other cancer experts the Guardian has spoken to believe there will be efficiencies for treatment, diagnostics and pathology services that will bear fruit, heralding more personalised and more equitable cancer care.

Cancer is not a single disease. It’s a catch-all term that describes the uncontrollable growth of abnormal cells. Typically, we describe cancers based on the location within the body that they are found: breast, prostate, lung, brain, blood, pancreas. These are complex, highly variable diseases, affecting a variety of different cells and underpinned by a host of genetic changes. In addition, cancer outcomes depend on many factors, including the biology of the disease and the treatments available. A single cure for cancer is not only unlikely but nigh on impossible.

Just take the brain. Though not all are cancerous, “there are more than 100 types of tumours in the brain, much more than in any other single organ”, says Felix Sahm, a neuropathologist at the University Hospital Heidelberg. “There are so many unresolved questions in brain tumour research and brain tumour care.”

We’ve made great leaps in cancer survival rates over the past century; chemotherapy and radiation have enabled solid tumours to be cured, monoclonal antibodies ushered in more direct targeting of abnormal cells, and emerging treatments are rewriting how we combat the disease. But, as Loi notes, “Human disease is very complex.” So where does AI fit in?

“AI can improve several parts of that process by helping us identify risk, detect disease, characterise tumours, select treatments and monitor,” says Ajit Goenka, a radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.

Medical imaging, in particular, stands to benefit from advances in AI and machine-learning models. Training models on huge amounts of patient data, such as CT scans, X-rays or tissue samples, enables those models to detect changes or patterns that may be imperceptible to the human eye.

Goenka has been exploring the early detection of pancreatic cancer with machine-learning tools since 2021, before the release of ChatGPT fully turned the public’s head toward generative AI. Since then, OpenAI and its rival Anthropic have pushed into new realms beyond chatbots: partnering with companies to accelerate access to treatment; striking deals with research centres; and working with pharmaceutical companies to incorporate large language models and AI into drug discovery.

Goenka noticed that some patients who developed pancreatic cancer had undergone CT scans months or years before diagnosis. Those scans were interpreted as normal but Goenka reasoned there could be microscopic, measurable changes invisible to a radiologist. “We began studying whether quantitative imaging and machine-learning methods could detect that signal,” he says.

In a proof-of-concept paper published in 2022, he confirmed that hunch. Machine-learning tools can detect pancreatic tumours, including in pancreases that appeared normal, before clinical diagnosis. Further studies by Goenka’s group have explored how robust and reproducible the method is and whether it is useful across institutions. The opportunity, he says, is to identify evidence of cancer earlier. My grandmother’s pancreatic cancer appeared as if out of nowhere, a shadow on a scan. Goenka’s models may have been able to see it sooner, which could have improved her outcome.

Sahm leads a European multi-disciplinary collaboration called EUcanAI, which is using agentic AI to improve the way brain tumours and central nervous system cancers are treated. The idea is that “every single chunk of this journey gets informed by the previous one and informs the next one in the sequence, so that it gets more efficient, quicker and less cumbersome for a patient”, he says.

He provides one example of a teenager who presented with a tumour in his brain stem. The expectation was that it was fatal, based on imaging and the patient’s age. The patient went in for surgery, his tumour was biopsied and rapidly sequenced to determine the mutations driving his disease.

Traditionally, these results go to a board of specialists to discuss the next steps in surgery and treatment. But today, these results can be delivered during a surgery, saving patients time and money. Sahm imagines a world where agentic AI accelerates this process even further – a surgeon could biopsy and image a tumour, then have an AI provide answers about the kind of mutation and potential drugs that may treat it. Sahm says this work is already happening in trials but stresses it is not yet routine.

The key for Sahm is a more tailored journey for each patient that “reduces the duration of uncertainty”. It’s about providing a wholly optimised approach to managing a patient’s cancer journey. He also notes it could provide more patients with better care.

This was a common thread in discussing AI tools for cancer diagnostics. “I think it will help with regards to equity of care, and access to care,” Loi says.

For instance, she says, in rural communities or locations that do not have cancer facilities or access to specialists or specialist diagnostic tools, access to machine-learning models could help medical professionals provide faster, more complete answers.

The dream of curing cancer is one that big AI firms constantly seed. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, has suggested that within a decade, cancer – and many other diseases – could be cured. The Google DeepMind spin-off, IsoLabs, has a bold mission statement to “solve” all disease.

Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, has similar lofty goals, suggesting the ability to solve disease might just be a problem of how much computing power backs our AI systems. “Maybe with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer,” he wrote. As AI firms experience growing backlash to the environmental cost of datacentres, the argument that just a little more compute could offer life-saving opportunities could be hard to sell.

But Emilia Javorsky, a physician and scientist at the Future of Life Institute, argues the opposite: “We cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure it.”

In her March essay on AI and cancer, she outlines the complicated process of developing and testing any new medication. “Thirteen years into the AI drug discovery movement, we still lack a single [Federal Drug Authority]-approved drug that cleared the full bar of regulatory approval, reimbursement, and clinical adoption,” she says.

Javorsky argues that curing cancer is a noble goal but the research community must be smart about where investment goes. It’s not intelligence that limits progress but the data, regulation and incentives that surround cancer research.

Even if all the data from research across the world was placed into these models, would that be enough to solve these diseases today? What about in five or 10 years? For Sahm, there are biological truths we are yet to uncover. In his work, he still encounters rare, unknown pathology that doesn’t “fit into a box”. While AI may be able to devise technology or tools to understand rare subtypes, it’s only as good as its training data.

The complexity of human physiology and biological processes comes up a lot in discussions with those working in cancer. Although AI may speed up the process of, for instance, hypothesising and creating new drugs that can treat specific forms of cancer, it is fundamentally limited in applying those learnings to the real world. “Someone actually has to go back and do the experiment, right?” Loi says.

An article published in The Australian newspaper in March revealed that a Sydney data scientist had been able to synthesise a bespoke cancer vaccine for his dog, Rosie, by uploading her genetic information to ChatGPT. And while some were astounded by the development, others noted that the hard work had still been done by humans in a lab.

Even if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape. Sahm notes that the majority of AI-assisted or AI-led research being performed is experimental and remains in clinical trials. Even if AI tools were deemed safe for test patients, he says, the EU lacks a clear regulatory path to allow them to reach the market. “That ends up in a lot of AI research going on, a lot of surprising and promising things happening … but also surprisingly few of those really being applied,” he says.

The most vocal proponents of AI – those building the models – may make grand claims about cures but on the ground the reality is different. There’s a lack of understanding of cancer complexity, many researchers working in the space argue.

But it’s clear that AI does provide a sense of hope for clinicians and researchers. Alone it cannot dethrone the king of terrors; it cannot bring down the emperor of all maladies. Curing cancer will require more than extra-efficient computation.

“AI can come up with a million hypotheses,” Loi says – but we will still need humans to help understand which of them are true.

“Technology,” says Goenka, “is only one part of the answer.”

fullText:
Independent outlets are leaning on social media, chat and other nontraditional methods to fight disinformation

When Allan Marrero, an asylum-seeker from the Cayman Islands, was released after five months in immigration detention, there was only one journalist he invited to his celebration: Eileen Grench, a reporter with the independent, non-profit news outlet Documented.

Grench had previously reported on Marrero, who was detained after interviewing with federal officials for a marriage-based green card. But beyond covering his detention struggles, she humanized him, emphasizing his and his husband’s love story.

“Most folks in these situations aren’t just victims; they’re fighting and being resilient and maintain the beautiful things about their life, too,” said Grench.

The Marreros’ trust in Grench and Documented resulted in full access and rich reporting that received much attention; even NYC’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, tweeted Grench’s story upon Allan’s release. “To see their story kind of lifted up on to that city stage was really gratifying,” Grench said.

Documented is one of many immigrant-serving news outlets across the US meeting the moment when many legacy and mainstream publications are not, whether due to layoffs, lack of resources or being out of touch with immigrant communities. These independent local news organizations are using social media, chat apps and other nontraditional methods to connect directly with immigrants and non-English speakers – especially during recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) surges – and they are leaving an impression.

“The impacts are phenomenal for relatively new media outlets, and part of it is because they’re operating on such a hyper-local level,” said Angie Chuang, a journalism professor at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Immigrant communities know what they need. They might not be able to access it or make it happen, but they can articulate their own needs. What these outlets are doing is just understanding how amplifying the community’s voices can help them.”

Last year, Documented and the Spanish-language news service Conecta Arizona launched the Immigrant News Coalition (INC) with the Listening Post Collective, the Bay Area’s El Tímpano, and the Minneapolis-based Sahan Journal to share strategies and resources for serving immigrant communities – and to ensure their outlets’ survival. Their work has since been bolstered by a $1.5m award from the Press Forward Foundation to “test and spread effective revenue models for immigrant-serving newsrooms” and additional funding from Democracy Fund.

Through listening tours and research, the outlets have found that members of immigrant communities in the US don’t always read the news by visiting websites and reading push notifications, especially when English is not their first language. Instead, they rely on other platforms that may have inaccurate information, such as WhatsApp, which over half of Latinos in the US use.

To meet specific immigrant communities where they are, Documented runs a WhatsApp group in Spanish, a WeChat group for Chinese immigrants, and a TikTok account in Haitian Creole to combat misinformation about ICE raids and fear-based scams.

“Misinformation thrives when there is a vacuum of good information, and immigrant communities are so vulnerable because of the lack of alternatives,” said Madeleine Bair, the founder of El Tímpano. “We’re not translating news into other languages. We’re creating news first and foremost for immigrant communities, and that looks very different than news created for non-immigrant communities.”

Emmy-winning journalist Maritza Félix started Conecta Arizona’s WhatsApp group, La Hora del Cafecito (Coffee Time), during the pandemic to provide timely, accurate news for immigrant communities in Spanish. The online gathering space, which has thousands of members across platforms, has a weekly Q&A with expert guests, including immigration attorneys, education policy experts and labor rights specialists.

But as ICE raids continue, members are engaging less in the public group chat and 

“They’re afraid of being a screenshot, or having their message forwarded to someone,” Félix said. “Listening to our community taught us that what works today might not work next week. We are listening to what they say and their silences at the same time.”

Having a dialogue with the local Bay Area immigrant community has been crucial for El Tímpano, which is Spanish for “eardrum”. In addition to SMS messaging that reaches more than 7,000 Spanish-speaking immigrants, the outlet’s disinformation defense initiative, Comunidades Informadas, has trained more than 400 Latino immigrants in the Bay Area to recognize and address disinformation and misinformation.

“By equipping immigrants with an understanding of how disinformation works, it can empower them, so that when they see a rumor of an ICE raid, their immediate response isn’t to panic,” Bair said. “Instead, they can check with a source they trust or call their local rapid response hotline. We’ve received really positive responses to these workshops and to the information that we provide to combat that fear.”

In May, the Alameda county library partnered with El Tímpano for a disinformation defense initiative workshop in Spanish via Zoom for its staff members. Attenders found the content easy to understand, and it helped them articulate how to identify disinformation not just to community members, but also to their own family members.

“After going through the workshop, I was like, ‘I can talk to this with my tia and my tios, and explain it to them in the way that I didn’t really have the language before,’” said Jaqueline Martinez, the Alameda county library’s equity services coordinator.

For many of these outlets, the work and impact started before the recent ICE surge. In 2019, Documented co-founders Mazin Sidahmed and Max Siegelbaum spoke with community organizations across New York that were concerned about workers’ wages being stolen. Joined later by reporter Lam Thuy Vo, they launched an investigation, seeking out New York state and federal wage data for four years. The result was Documented’s Wage Theft Monitor, which inspired NY state legislators to introduce three bills to prevent and punish wage theft.

“The dual impact of protecting immigrant workers, but also helping the general public understand how pervasive this issue is, has been one of the most rewarding parts of seeing this project come to light,” Sidahmed said.

Similarly, LA Taco, which isn’t part of the INC, originally built trust among Los Angeles immigrant communities through its coverage of food, culture and cannabis. Then last June, as ICE raids swept through Los Angeles, LA Taco journalist Memo Torres began posting daily recaps of ICE activity on the publication’s Instagram account. By reporting verified information about raids during a time when misinformation ran rampant, Torres became one of LA’s most trusted journalists for immigrant communities, increasing LA Taco’s membership from 1,500 to 77,000 and earning attention from state and federal government officials.

“I was getting information from people, I started reaching out to rapid responders and building trust with them, and then got included in the network with them,” he said, recalling how he started the Daily Memo.

Over the summer, the Daily Memo wound down, while LA Taco’s political cartoons by Pulitzer prize finalist Ivan Ehlers, called Sunday Taquitos, took off. In July, his humorous yet poignant illustration about Flock camera surveillance received more than 7m Instagram views and inspired fan-created versions in five different languages. The Ecuadorian American artist said the political cartoons are his short-form way of fighting misinformation and disinformation.

“If I can get someone’s attention for five seconds, I can get people to look at important issues and say, ‘Hey, I didn’t know that was happening. Oh man, this is terrible,’” he said. “People will go in and do more research, read more about it, talk to their friends or share it, and that’ll start conversations.”

Ehlers has also served as creative director for one of LA Taco’s zines, showcasing the outlet’s reporting on local protests and immigrant communities. Its release in early September was just one of many in-person events LA Taco has held this year to engage with its readers.

“The bigger issue is building a community and building support systems and showing people that they’re not alone,” Ehlers said. “We have a lot of people who are willing to fight together, work together and build something together.”

fullText:
The former UK deputy prime minister is a board member of the UK-based company and owns 917,000 shares

Nick Clegg could make approximately $40m (£30m) from the planned float of Nscale as the UK-based datacentre company prepares for a US stock market listing.

The former UK deputy prime minister owns more than 917,000 shares in the startup, which is reportedly seeking a valuation of up to $35bn in a flotation. Based on Clegg’s stake of 0.12%, that could yield a valuation of about $42m for the ex-Liberal Democrat party leader.

Clegg is a board member at Nscale along with the former Meta executive, Sheryl Sandberg, whose 0.25% stake could be worth $88m if Nscale floats at the $35bn valuation, a figure reported by the Financial Times this month.

However, Nscale was last valued in a funding round at $14.6bn, implying lower valuations of Clegg and Sandberg’s stakes of about $18m and $37m, respectively. Forbes has estimated Sandberg’s wealth at $2.4bn, while Clegg has made about £24m from sales of shares in Meta, where he was formerly the president of global affairs. Both are paid an annual retainer of $60,000.

The Telegraph first reported Clegg’s potential wealth gain from the Nscale float.

UK-based Nscale filed papers for its flotation in the US on 18 September and could make its stock market debut before the year end. The company is preparing to list in New York, reflecting its global ambitions and the depth of funding available in the US for expensive AI infrastructure projects.

Nscale reported a loss of $1bn in the six months to 30 June, on revenues of $140m. In the flotation document, Nscale said its losses reflected the “substantial investments” it has made in a “highly capital intensive” business.

Josh Payne, the chief executive of Nscale, has said the company sees a “significant” opportunity in sovereign AI, where countries develop their own models and infrastructure, in order to reduce reliance on US or Chinese technology.

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, and Margrethe Vestager, the former EU competition head, have both called for Europe to do more to develop its own AI infrastructure.

“Nscale is well positioned to serve this demand as a trusted, sovereign-capable platform,” said Payne. “This is particularly true in Europe, where the need for sovereign AI infrastructure is especially acute, and where our British domicile positions us as a natural, trusted partner.”

Nscale operates five datacentres in Europe and has a further 12 under different phases of construction including in the US. The Guardian revealed this year that one Nscale project in Loughton, Essex, is an undeveloped scrapyard.

Nscale has been approached for comment.

title: OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain
description: Former chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI...
fullText:
Former chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI tech

UK politics live – latest updates

Datacentre nimbys are holding Britain back, George Osborne has said in reaction to nationwide protests about the giant water- and energy-guzzling structures.

The former Tory chancellor is now the head of AI for countries at OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. His job is to represent the company to governments around the world and he also has a role in enabling the building of datacentres and other infrastructure.

Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Somerset on Sunday, Osborne said: “You try and build a datacentre in Britain … I spent my life when I was politician trying to get people to agree to have new roads and railway lines and airport runways, and communities go up in arms – it’s really hard to build a datacentre.”

He said the UK would lose its “sovereignty” over tech to the US if it failed to allow datacentres to be built.

He explained: “You can either choose to have these datacentres in Ohio and Georgia and Michigan, which is where they’re all being built … we don’t allow these things to be built. They’re going to be built elsewhere, and you know that’s a loss of some sovereign control over the physical location where these things are.”

There have been protests about datacentres across the UK, including in central London, Devon and outside Holyrood in Edinburgh. People have said they are a blight on the landscape, questioned whether they will bring jobs to the local area, and argued they will take investment and space that could be used for affordable housing. There are also concerns about the vast water and energy use.

The government has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure to get them built more quickly. But the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building them.

Osborne dismissed the concerns over datacentres as nimbyism. He said: “I think a lot of the to opposition datacentres is very much like ‘not in my back yard’. There’s an enormous building boom going on in the United States of datacentres, even as the political opposition undoubtedly is growing.”

Verity Harding, the head of the AI and geopolitics project at Cambridge University’s Bennett School for Public Policy, said people had wider concerns over these centres.

She said: “The reason everyone hates datacentres has nothing to do with datacentres. It’s the only tangible thing to protest against … [people] just don’t like what’s happening and they don’t feel that anybody’s in control or thinking about the impact of it.

“It’s exactly because the tech industry execs are talking in this ridiculous way … You know, you cannot go out on the one hand and say this [AI] might kill everybody one week and then the next week go and appear at a big sales conference saying that you should integrate it into your business.”

Bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest AI companies, will be meeting world leaders at the UN general assembly in New York City this week amid debate over the prospect of dangerous, superintelligent AI and whether and how it should be regulated.

Osborne said: “The fact that corporate leaders are sitting down with the presidents and prime ministers of the world in the UN security council I would say actually shouldn’t be alarming. It’s actually reassuring that people are beginning to try and use the kind of institutions of the world to think about how we regulate this new technology.”

title: Using AI to ‘talk to animals’ might make us feel clever – but what, if anything, does it do for them?
description:
As animal behaviorists increasingly use AI in their research, they grapple with how to wield the technology responsibly

The motor is off, the turquoise sea is glassy, and Stephanie King and I are motionless, transfixed by the whistles, clicks and squeezy, whirring noises made by the dolphins swimming below us.
If anyone could tell me what these big-brained social mammals are saying, it would be her. Based at the University of Bristol, she co-leads Shark Bay Dolphin Research, one of the longest-running wild dolphin research projects in the world. She has spent thousands of hours watching and listening to this population.
fullText:
I’m sitting in a small boat in Shark Bay, Australia, eavesdropping on a conversation between some of Earth’s most intelligent beings. The motor is off, the turquoise sea is glassy, and Stephanie King and I are motionless, transfixed by the whistles, clicks and squeezy, whirring noises made by the dolphins swimming below us.

If anyone could tell me what these big-brained social mammals are saying, it would be her. Based at the University of Bristol, she co-leads Shark Bay Dolphin Research, one of the longest-running wild dolphin research projects in the world. She has spent thousands of hours watching and listening to this population.

Like most other animal behaviorists, King is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence into her research process. “If it’s used responsibly, AI can transform what we can do with the data we collect,” she says. But when I ask her if AI will someday allow us to “speak dolphin”, she stiffens a little. “I think we’re doing the animals a disservice by focusing on that question,” she says.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/1_Dolphins_Chit-chat_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

Dolphins communicate, navigate and find food using buzzes, pops, whistles and other acoustic signals. These sounds were recorded in Shark Bay, western Australia via an underwater microphone by Amy Martin for the podcast Threshold

The problem, King says, is not AI itself, but the narrative being built around it. She sees her field increasingly framed as a quest for an AI-assisted animal interpreter, with headlines declaring that we’ve almost “cracked the secret language” of various creatures or are about to “decode animals’ speech”. There are even cash prizes for breakthroughs, including the Coller Dolittle Challenge, which seeks an algorithm for communicating with non-human organisms.

“It’s a sexy topic,” King acknowledges, but in her view, fundamentally misguided. She believes the allure of tech dollars and media attention is priming the pump of research in some unhealthy ways – nudging scientists to make premature claims about AI-assisted findings, and encouraging them to describe their work in sensational terms. “They tend to be biasing themselves towards the most exciting discovery,” says King, which “misleads us to what we know about these animals”.

What we know, in many cases, is in fact very little. Take dolphins. “They’ve been studied for decades, but we’re still scratching the surface with what many of the sounds mean,” King says. Sound itself likely means something different to dolphins than it does to us. They can detect pitches far outside our range of hearing, they process acoustic information much faster than we do, and our sensory systems are wired differently in important ways.

For example, both humans and dolphins can echolate – or use sound to navigate – but dolphins process echolocation information in the part of the brain connected to touch, while for us, it’s more connected to vision. In other words, instead of “seeing” with sound, dolphins might be hear-feeling, or feel-hearing, their way through their watery world. Whatever that experience is, it may be fundamentally inaccessible to us – and it’s not something we can comprehend by plugging their whistles and squeaks into a large language model. “We need to appreciate that they have a complex communication system that we barely understand,” says King. She believes our focus should be learning about that system – piecing together what dolphin behavior and communication means to other dolphins – rather than trying to hack into it, and start a conversation.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/2_Dolphins_Whistles_Credit_Stephanie_King_-_Shark_Bay_Dolphin_Research.mp3

These high-pitched whistles are a very important part of dolphins’ social communication. Mothers use them to keep in contact with their calves and some whistles are even used as individual identifiers, or name-like calls. Credit: Stephanie King, Shark Bay Dolphin Research

Elephant researcher Joyce Poole agrees. “I get quite exasperated by this goal of being able to talk to the animals,” she says. “I think it’s kind of gimmicky.” One of the world’s leading experts on African savanna elephants, Poole has spent decades observing the animals in the wild, building up a treasure trove of annotated field recordings of their vocalizations, movements and interactions. She’s convinced that there are many layers and nuances of elephant communication that we don’t yet understand, but, like King, she’s skeptical about the concept of inserting ourselves into their dialogues. “Just the basic ability to understand what they have to say and what they are thinking about – that’s enough for me,” she says. “I don’t need to interfere in their lives more than necessary.”

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/6_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_1_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp3

Joyce Poole has documented female elephants making these overlapping sounds when a musth male arrives in their group, looking to breed. She refers to the sounds as “Female Chorus Rumbles” and they may include snorts, trumpets and roars, as well as low-pitched rumbles. Credit: The Elephant Ethogram, ElephantVoices

At the same time, Poole believes making the inner lives of elephants more legible to humans could transform how we treat them. “I hope that by showing that they’re capable of a more sophisticated kind of communication that we gain them some respect from our fellow humans, and save a place for them in the world, together with their ecosystems and their other fellow travelers,” she says.

Poole’s hope is widely shared, and is likely one of the main reasons so many of us are prone to click on stories with headlines about how AI is going to help us talk to animals. As extinction numbers rise and biodiversity declines, we’re desperate for some good news. Humans are also inherently fascinated by other animals; we’ve been telling stories about listening to and learning from them for as long as we’ve walked the Earth. Our technologies have in many ways cut us off from the rest of the living world – could this be a case when a new tool helps us to better tune into and care for our planetmates?

“I do see AI as a potentially promising avenue for knowing more, and understanding better, non-human animal lives,” says César Rodríguez-Garavito, founding director of the More Than Human Life (Moth) program at NYU, a leading hub for research and discourse on the rights of nature. He thinks AI could help give animals a voice in the decisions that shape their lives.

“More and more researchers and practitioners are asking themselves, ‘Well, how do we bring in the voices of, say, the whales in the regulation of a marine-protected area,’” he says. It may sound far-fetched to us now, but Rodríguez-Garavito says attempts to bring non-human voices into the realms of law and policy are already under way in countries around the world. “I think that this is no longer a science fiction question,” he says. Of course, we don’t need AI to tell us that whales are being negatively impacted by noise, ship strikes, climate disruption and pollution, but perhaps if we heard a direct translation of them expressing pain from underwater seismic testing, or mourning the loss of a calf killed by a ship, we would be more likely to act.

“But I cannot speak about potential benefits without speaking about risks,” Rodríguez-Garavito says. “We have, as human beings, a very mixed track record, to put it gently, in using technologies.” That record tells us that we can’t simply deploy AI in the wild and see what happens; we need to think through the risks ahead of time. There’s the possibility of intentional harm, like using AI-powered tools to trick or coerce animals, perhaps moving them into areas where they’re easier to kill (“I mean, think of trophy hunters,” says Poole). But if the past predicts the future, the greatest threats are not a few people using a new technology with malicious intent, but a whole lot of us using it without thinking about – or choosing to care about – the consequences.

“The nightmare scenario is one where we interrupt their communications and their lives at will, just for our entertainment,” says Rodríguez-Garavito. It’s not hard to imagine whale-watching companies using AI to lure animals toward boats, for example, or visitors to Yellowstone national park using apps to provoke wolves to howl, elk to bugle, or bison to bellow, exhausting and confusing the animals. Technologies are not beholden to the intentions of their makers. A tool created with the sincere goal of enhancing our respect for animals could end up having the opposite effect by turning them into playthings that we can pester and control.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/3_Dolphins_Researchers_in_the_field_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

Researchers Stephanie King and Laura Palmer document the movements and behaviors of a group of dolphins in Shark Bay. Buzzes and whistles from the dolphins are being picked up by underwater microphones and played through a speaker on the boat. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

In an attempt to help steer the field away from these dark scenarios, the Moth program recently published the Pepp framework (prepare, engage, prevent and protect), a set of ethical guidelines for the use of non-human animal communication technologies. But if and how it will actually get put into practice is uncertain. Rodríguez-Garavito says this is a trickle-down effect of the larger absence of legal and ethical boundaries around AI development. “At this point, there is no international agreement on AI,” he says. “It is a free-for-all. I would be much less concerned if we had general principles on what can and cannot be done with AI. There’s nothing like that, and this is why we’re having to develop them from scratch based on what’s been done in other fields of legal practice.”

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/7_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_2_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp3

Mickey Pardo, who works with Joyce Poole as a senior scientist at ElephantVoices, also sees potential benefits and risks of AI-assisted animal communication tools, but he also wonders if the speculation is a bit overblown on both sides. “Playbacks can be stressful for animals even without AI – when you’re just taking prerecorded sounds and playing them back – especially if you don’t know the context of those sounds,” he says. Maybe a more sophisticated AI version could add to that stress, but Pardo sees it more as turning up the dial on a problem we already have, versus opening an entirely new can of worms.

He also questions whether we’re focusing too much on possible harms from AI when there are so many other ways we negatively impact animals’ lives, including in research settings.

“The way that animals are treated in biomedical science is so incredibly horrific compared to anything that anybody’s doing in the field of animal communication,” he says. “Not that we shouldn’t be thinking about the ethical implications [of AI] ahead of time. I just worry that perhaps we’re sucking up too much oxygen worrying about a hypothetical ethical problem when there are many very real, present ethical problems that we’re essentially ignoring.”

 This oxygen-sucking, mesmerizing effect of AI – the attention and money poured toward it, and the almost magical powers we’re willing to ascribe to it – also concerns marine mammal researcher Luke Rendell, based at the University of St Andrews. “There’s been this idea put about that AI is going to find something that we couldn’t,” he says. “It’s something of a confidence trick, I think.”

Rendell believes the AI hype has gotten way ahead of the science, and that the public is being led to believe that we know – or are about to know – much more than we actually do about animal communication. For example, Earth Species Project claims on their website that “with exponential advances in AI and Large Language Models, decoding animal communication is no longer a question of if – it’s when” and states that they have already found support for their hypothesis that “AI can decode the shared structures of language across the Tree of Life”.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/4_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describing_context_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

King says AI can be a very helpful tool when used in the right ways, but spending time with the animals in their habitat is essential for understanding what their vocal communication means to them. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

This is the sort of framing that gives Rendell hives. Like Stephanie King, he believes pursuing a quest to reveal the “language” of animals is loaded with humancentric bias that could actually limit our understanding of their unique and wildly diverse ways of getting their messages across. He’s also concerned about long-term damage to his field when the Dr Dolittle machine fails to materialize.

The study of animal communication has attracted a fair number of charlatans over the years, leading to boom-and-bust cycles of funding and credibility. Rendell says he entered the field of cetacean communication “just as it was recovering from a 15-year hangover” from the work of John Lilly, whose efforts to teach dolphins English using controversial methods – like giving them LSD – brought Lilly a lot of fame, but ultimately led to nothing but a tragic end for one of the dolphins at the center of his experiments. For more than a decade after that, the study of dolphin communication was “the punchline of a joke in scientific circles”. says Rendell, but “we’ve had this flowering in the last 15 to 20 years of understanding and knowledge about cetacean society and communication”, which he says has “taken the whole field on to a new level of credibility. And my main fear is that it is being undermined by these irresponsible claims.”

King says it all comes back to testing any AI findings with the experts: the animals themselves. “I think you have to use these AI and machine learning approaches alongside careful examination of the animals: when they produce calls, and in what context, and how they behave,” she says. This is patient, painstaking work that requires careful studies in the field, often conducted over years – the opposite of Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” ethos.

Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/5_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describes_sound_production_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp3

Dolphins detect sound waves through their lower jaws and produce sounds through the top of their heads. King describes how that works as buzzes made by a nearby dolphin are picked up by underwater microphones. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

The days I spent on the water with King involved a lot of quiet waiting, scanning the horizon for the glint of dolphins rising to the surface. When we spotted an animal, King would immediately beginning calling out names – Juicy, Jungle, Piccolo – while the scientists-in-training on the boat with us snapped photographs and took notes. King can identify hundreds of individual dolphins after the briefest glimpse of their dorsal fins, a skill she attributes to the countless hours she has spent in Shark Bay, observing the animals on site. “I come every year, and it’s a really important part of my life,” she says.

She also believes it’s a really important part of doing good science. When they return from the field, her students will spend time looking through the photographs of the fins, matching them to pictures from previous years in their dolphin “look book”. King says lately some students have been asking her to let AI do that work. It would, of course, be much faster. But she insists they do it manually. “If you really want to understand behavior, then the details matter,” she says. “And the details take time. You can’t rush it.”

Meanwhile, a larger question looms for all of us: as exciting as it might be to imagine walking around with an animal translator in our pockets, do we have to wait for new technology to pay more attention to our planetmates? Because whether or not AI ever allows us to talk with animals, there’s nothing stopping us from listening to them, and caring about their lives.

Amy Martin is the founder and executive producer of Threshold, a Peabody award-winning documentary podcast. She is now writing her first book

title: Trump Wants to Keep Journalists Out of the White House. He Should Get His Wish.
description: Chris...
fullText:
The president has banned MS NOW, CNN, and Politico from attending press briefings. The rest of the media should respond with a boycott.

At a loss to assert persuasive control over the cooling economy, the dismal and nonsensical war in Iran, the runaway development of AI, or the food supply, President Donald Trump has reverted to the conservative movement’s go-to culture-war refrain: demonizing the media. In an overheated Truth Social post late last week, Trump announced that he was revoking the clearances of CNN, Politico, and MS NOW to continue attending White House briefings. Sure enough, reporters from those outlets found their access to the White House blocked when they tried to gain entry. The targeted news organizations have announced that they will sue the Trump administration for depriving them of basic First Amendment freedoms.

That action is a sound and time-honored line of defense for news outlets facing the specter of prior restraint from the executive branch. Yet Trump’s unconstitutional blacklist move—which he vowed would be but the opening salvo in his administration’s press inquisition—creates an opening to finally chloroform the desiccated ritual of the White House press briefing. The time is ripe for a full boycott of the Trump agitprop spectacle from every news organization in America. The decision by TV networks to suspend pool coverage of the White House is a good first step in this direction, but the simple truth of the matter is that the American press can only regain its independence by quitting the White House briefing room once and for all.

Like the embarrassingly compromised annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, the briefing has long outlived any notional journalistic purpose it might have once served. Going back to Ron Ziegler’s reign as enfant terrible of the messaging arm of the Nixon White House, the briefings have always functioned chiefly as culture-war theater, allowing presidents and press secretaries to browbeat correspondents for raising questions that contradict their ideological power scripts, while granting showboating network correspondents in the Sam Donaldson vein quick and viral opportunities to be seen haranguing administration flacks in a brightly lit intellectual vacuum. In many ways, Trump’s bid to limit exchanges in the briefing room to exercises in ideologically vetted rightthink is but the logical limit-case of the Faustian bargain that’s fueled the briefing room’s operations for decades.

Prior to Trump’s power grab, the Oval Office deference of the White House briefing reached its purest form in the George W. Bush White House, when the president made a point of icing out UPI correspondent Helen Thomas, a fierce critic of the invasion of Iraq, from any recognition from the podium for three years. That petulant display of favoritism spoke volumes about what the briefings were meant to accomplish: patrician indulgences for mainstream correspondents willing to toe the party line, and pariahdom for any hapless dissenter. For Bush, it worked—the White House press corps was content to sit on its hands as the administration treated Thomas like a dirty hippie, and they continued parroting the administration’s Iraq War fantasias to epically calamitous effect.

In his own vendetta against the White House press corps, Trump has merely turned this tactic up to 11, punishing any news outlet that has inadvertently stood athwart his own bottomless store of imagined grievance. (His decision to banish CNN is especially rich, since under the watch of its moronic former CEO Jeff Zucker the cable networked devoted acres of unfiltered coverage to Trump’s 2016 campaign—a virtual in-kind donation that worked out to roughly $2 billion across the industry, as other witless executives followed Zucker’s lead.)

Of course, the news organizations currently battling to reclaim their spots in the briefing room aren’t likely to sign on to the mission to abolish it altogether. Just for starters, they’d be loath to surrender the status and convenience of a perch within the White House—and TV news outfits in particular aren’t likely to surrender the cheap optics furnished by theatrical bantering with a president or his designated press flacks. But in substantive journalistic terms, there’s nothing to be gained by continuing this Kabuki theater of imperial press-corps respectability. Especially under an administration that has made the pursuit of empirical truth a de facto thought crime, no civic purpose is served by sending out network anchorbots en masse to field its lies. And once we’ve dispensed with the briefings, we can embark on a long-overdue recalibration of the logic of White House coverage.

Instead of passively conniving in the bid to remake the White House press corps in the image of Bari Weiss’s CBS News, news organizations can hold administration officials truly accountable by drawing on contributions from people who actually know something about key policy calls. In lieu of airing an endless regress of breathless will-they-won’t-they accounts of Federal Reserve rate hikes or focusing on Wall Street’s instant reaction, press outlets could have actual economists assess the likely impact of the Fed’s decision-making in the real economy. Or as Russell Vought seeks the authority to administer and strike down research grants at the National Institute of Health, news organizations can track the fallout on a whole series of fronts, from cancer treatments to public health to longevity. Climate journalists could, at long last, be in a position to foreground the global catastrophe that the Trump administration is fomenting by treating climate change as a hoax.

Major news organizations did refuse, after all, to take part in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s effort to turn Pentagon press corps into an agitprop subsidiary, and there’s been no fall-off in crucial coverage of his woeful term in office. Indeed, GOP Representative Thomas Massie’s motion to impeach Hegseth, which spooked MAGA-prostrate House Speaker Mike Johnson into calling the chamber into an early fall recess, drew extensively on press accounts that documented Hegseth’s unfitness for office in scarifying detail, from the Defense Department’s campaign of murder in the Southern Hemisphere to the Pentagon’s shameful effort to conceal American fatalities in the Iran war. Let the members of the White House press corps heed this example, and start exercising actual journalistic independence—together with the ability to genuinely think and research for themselves.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

Trump, Greenland and Denmark to sign deal in bid to end Arctic standoff
description:
-Pedersen 
   COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is due to meet with leaders of Greenland and Denmark on Tuesday to sign a deal that will allow a larger ‌US military presence on Greenland and could end a standoff over the strategically located and ‌mineral-rich island. 
   The agreement will allow the US to expand its military footprint in Greenland, three people familiar with the matter have told ​Reuters. 
   In addition to the existing Pituffik Space Base, the deal is expected to open two new military sites: Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War airbase whose population has dwindled to just a few dozen, and Mestersvig, currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, an elite Danish special forces unit. 
   Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous ‌territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, ⁠sits between the Arctic and North America and holds vast energy resources. 
   Trump's refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire it triggered a diplomatic crisis in ⁠January within NATO and forced Denmark and the island's government into intensive negotiations.
fullText:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and the leaders of ‌Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement on Tuesday that ‌permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a ​standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island.

The agreement, signed during Trump's visit to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Trump's demand that the US adopt Greenland as ‌a US territory to ⁠head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China.

But the deal does permit a greater ⁠US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover.

In his ​speech to ​the assembled world leaders at ​the UN before the signing ‌ceremony, Trump said the agreement gives the US "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory."

"No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express ‌written approval," Trump said.

Trump signed the ​agreement along with Danish Prime Minister ​Mette Frederiksen and Greenland ​Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen in a trilateral ceremony ‌after Trump gave his UN ​speech.

Frederiksen described the ​agreement as "a deal that can "last forever" and said it underlines the importance of the NATO alliance and respects Greenland's ​right to self-determination.

(Reporting ‌by Gram Slattery at the UN and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen ​in Copenhagen; Writing by Steve Holland; Editing Xevi Fontdegloria, ​Ross Colvin and Rosalba O'Brien)

fullText:
Yemen's Houthis accused Saudi Arabia on Tuesday of launching a wave of deadly strikes that killed civilians and prison inmates, as Riyadh seeks to repel an offensive that has seen the Iran-backed group seize strategic territory.

The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast has left hundreds dead and heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

It has also forced thousands to flee, with the United Nations on Tuesday forecasting the number of displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.

The gains made by the Houthis have cemented the hold of Iran and its regional allies over two key waterways in the Middle East -- and the straits of Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz -- which are major shipping arteries for global flows of energy.

Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally-recognised government, has sought to contain the Houthi advance with airstrikes.

The Houthis have retaliated with attacks on Saudi territory, including a strike targeting the capital Riyadh for the first time in years.

The strike came days after Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting the holy city of Mecca, though the fighters denied the claim.

In a rare statement, Saudi King Salman praised the armed forces and security services for defending the country, and condemned the alleged attempt to target Mecca, calling it "a provocation to Muslims around the world", and branded the Houthis a "terrorist militia".

In Yemen, the Houthis said a strike on a prison killed nine detainees, while they also accused the Saudis of killing six civilians including two children in the port city of Mocha.

Two more civilians were killed by strikes in Yemen's Al-Jawf province, the Houthis added.

"A mother and child were killed, while her husband and two of her other children were wounded in strikes carried out by the Saudi enemy" in the Al-Batin area, Houthi media said, citing the Houthi health ministry.

As violence has escalated, thousands of families have been forced from their homes, many for a second or third time.

"I hope I can find a house to live in with my children. We're exhausted by the heat, the dust and the humiliation," Arwa, a mother of four children, told AFP at a camp for displaced people near Aden.

The Middle East war began in February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which prompted the Islamic republic to retaliate with attacks around the region and by mobilising its allies.

While the Yemen civil war predates the broader regional conflict, it has become its most active front in recent days.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has in the past two days killed 154 people, military sources from both sides told AFP.

"The death toll from Saudi airstrikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118," Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their ranks.

Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency on Tuesday issued a warning of potential danger in the country's south near the Yemen border, the first alert since the Houthis launched their attack on Riyadh over the weekend.

The alert, which asked people to remain indoors and avoid open areas, was lifted a short while later.

G7 leaders representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States called on the Houthis to "immediately cease all military actions".

They also demanded the Houthis end "all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith", while urging Tehran "to end its arming of and support for the Houthis".

Britain has agreed to provide some military support to Saudi Arabia, defence minister Luke Pollard said, while France also pledged to help secure Saudi energy infrastructure, a diplomatic source told AFP.

But "this in no way involves taking part in the conflict with the Houthis", the French source said.

The Houthis have carried out attacks against facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Yemen's government and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have reportedly requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis.

On Tuesday in New York, Trump was due to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The GCC, in which Saudi Arabia plays an outsized role, has in the past urged Trump against further escalation in the war with Iran.

title: GOP shifts midterm priorities as concerns turn to defending seats in red states
description: Republicans are playing defense deep in their own territory as voter anger over price hikes puts more House and Senate seats in play in the midterms.
fullText:
Republicans are playing defense deep in their own territory as voter anger over price hikes puts more House and Senate seats in play in the midterms.

New rounds of big spending, visits from Trump administration officials and private conversations among top GOP officials overseeing the battle for control of Congress reveal a party rushing to shore up red seats and states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024.

In the House, the fight has expanded far outside the few-dozen seats considered the most competitive as Republicans start to unleash their massive warchest: Since Aug. 1, more than $110 million in ad bookings have gone toward Republican-held districts so red that Trump won them by double digits.

In the Senate, Republicans are racing to shore up Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted as the Midwest struggles under the weight of Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices. Trump and Vice President JD Vance are both expected to travel to the state before the midterms to boost Husted, according to four people familiar with the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss not-yet-public plans.

GOP leaders are also trying to keep a handle on contests in Iowa and Kansas — and they've quietly begun deprioritizing Georgia and even North Carolina, which a growing number of Republicans are privately bracing for Democrats to flip.

"We need to stop the contagion," said one senior GOP official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the midterm landscape.

"The map is hilariously big right now," said one national Republican pollster.

Since Aug. 1, nearly two-thirds of advertising funds in House races have been booked or spent in races with GOP incumbents, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising.

That includes nearly $18 million to embattled Rep. Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District; $14.6 million to Texas' 15th District where Monica De La Cruz faces a challenge from Tejano Singer Bobby Pulido; $9.6 million in Alaska where Rep. Nick Begich faces a challenge from independent Bill Hill; and millions more to other districts that Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

The GOP holds a massive cash advantage over Democrats — which, for now, means they can afford to spend more broadly. Republican groups are dividing up the spending deluge in the final weeks ahead of the midterms, with Trump's MAGA Inc. affiliated super PAC spending heavily to shore up safer red seats and deter Democrats from pushing into those races.

"The voter enthusiasm [for Republican voters] is not where it needs to be but that's where a money advantage can make a really big impact," said Mark Bednar, a GOP strategist and former communications director for then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

Republicans have adjusted their Senate map expectations: They're still bullish about Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. They're not as optimistic about North Carolina — which Trump won in 2024 — but they are hoping to force Democrats to spend more there.

Republicans are more concerned about Alaska and Texas. And their worries about Ohio have escalated amid soaring diesel prices and backlash to tariffs — challenges they're also confronting in Texas, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas.

Already two battleground candidates have called for ends to the Iran war, pointing to the high prices: Iowa GOP Senate nominee Ashley Hinson, whose team has grown increasingly wary of the tight race and Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers. Both Hinson and Rogers use top Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio to guide their campaigns.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Hinson's and Rogers' remarks.

Senior GOP operatives' own internal polling shows Trump's approval underwater in deep red states across the country. And an Iowa poll conducted last week by a Democratic-leaning pollster found Democrat Josh Turek with a one-point lead in the Senate race and Trump's approval at 43 percent in the state he won by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, according to a copy of the poll obtained by POLITICO.

"As more races come online, it very clearly is a defensive map for Republicans across the country," said a national GOP strategist working on multiple battleground races.

In Ohio, Republicans are optimistic that their attacks on former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown's voting record are starting to break through, based on recent internal polling. But they've been conveying to outside groups for weeks that they need help reinforcing vulnerable incumbents like Husted. On Monday, the pro-crypto super PAC Fairshake said it planned to unleash $30 million against Brown, who was the top Democrat on the Banking Committee before losing reelection in 2024 — fueled in part by more than $40 million against him from Fairshake that year.

"The stakes go far beyond one Senate seat," Amy Natoce, a Husted campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. "Control of the Senate will determine which agenda moves forward in Washington: Sherrod Brown's out-of-touch socialist agenda, or Jon Husted's agenda of lower taxes, a secure border, and an economy that rewards hard work."

One Michigan Republican acknowledged the immense weight of the tariffs in races across the battleground state — including in the marquee Senate contest between Rogers and progressive Abdul El-Sayed, as well as across competitive House races.

"Everywhere we go, we are getting hammered on it," the Michigan Republican said. "It's crushing us."

Even skeptical Republicans have been quietly checking in with their colleagues to see if the panic in redder territory is borne out in reality on the ground or just overblown polling. One GOP lawmaker who spoke to Hinson and her campaign team was somewhat surprised by their answers.

"It's real," that House Republican told POLITICO.

And POLITICO overheard a senior member of Kansas' Republican party leadership complaining about their state's tighter-than-expected race at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, the person said, was in some trouble even as Republicans tried to dismiss the seriousness of his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton.

Trump and Vance, meanwhile, continue to travel to states they won by double digits in 2024 to stump for Republican candidates, as Trump-aligned super PACs hammer the airwaves in far more red territory than blue.

Recently-formed super PACs aligned with MAGA Inc. — Trump's main spending vehicle that holds more than $400 million — have spent in 42 House districts so far, 30 defensive and 12 offensive. On average, they are spending in areas that voted for Trump by 7.9 points in 2024, according to a POLITICO analysis.

The PACs are even spending in some districts Trump carried by 15 points as a way to shore up Republicans and deter Democratic advances, according to Republicans involved in the conversations.

Major Republican super PACs, including the Trump aligned-super PACs and party-linked groups, have spent in more than two dozen GOP-held seats where Trump won by at least 5 points in 2024.

"Republicans aren't taking anything for granted this cycle and will deploy whatever resources necessary to protect our majorities and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement.

The NRSC argued that "Democrats lack quality candidates and a clear path to victory," so the party is "feigning optimism" and looking to candidates who have lost before, including Brown, "to somehow deliver [a] majority." The NRCC said their opposition is "too broke to fight back."

The geography of the Senate map still favors the GOP this cycle: Democrats have to defend all of their seats, while flipping four Republican-held ones, to take control of the upper chamber.

Republicans believe they have a real shot at flipping New Hampshire, and public polling shows Minnesota's Senate race closer than expected, forcing Democrats to pay some minor attention to a state Kamala Harris won in 2024.

And Republicans are still hopeful that their mid-decade gerrymandering push could still give them a structural advantage as they fight to defend the House. Republicans won the redistricting war that erupted last summer and will likely net at least six seats from it.

But as economic concerns continue to dominate — with little relief in sight — Democrats are growing increasingly bullish.

"You know, I look at places like Kansas where I never thought we'd have a chance, or South Carolina or even Mississippi, these places are longshots, but they look like they're competitive," Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said.

For their part, senior Republicans have been working the problem from two ends, trying to gently persuade Trump in private conversations to back off some of his recent policy moves and wind down the war in Iran — while also organizing a wave of cash reinforcements across the growing map to try to stem the bleeding.

GOP lawmakers pressed Trump officials at their Dallas convention and since then to take emergency actions around fuel prices and refinery capacity. A band of House Republicans led an unsuccessful attempt to vote on a federal gas tax suspension until after Election Day. And, over the weekend, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) posted several direct appeals to Trump, asking why he hasn't put an embargo on diesel exports.

But many are convinced the bleeding won't stop until voters get some relief at the pump.

"The question is: How much longer can we go?" one senior House Republican said.
