fullText:
Our long, hot summer is finally coming to an end this evening with the autumnal equinox, which marks the beginning of fall here in the Northern Hemisphere.

At a precise moment each September, usually on the 22nd or 23rd, the sun is directly above the equator, marking the autumnal equinox in the Northern Hemisphere.

(South of the equator in the Southern Hemisphere, it's known as the vernal or spring equinox and marks the beginning of spring.)

But what weather will the U.S. see this fall, given the record hot August and a forecast that calls for El Niño to peak either in late fall or early winter?

Read on for the forecast and also a look back at some of the statistics that made the three-month summer so remarkable.

The exact time of the equinox is 8:05 p.m. ET. The equinox occurs at the same moment worldwide.

The word equinox comes from the Latin words "aequalis" and "nox," meaning equal night. On the autumnal (and the spring) equinox, day and night are both roughly 12 hours long in most of the world.

This will be true Sept. 22 from as far north as Utqiagvik (formerly Barrow), Alaska – north of the Arctic Circle – to as far south as Wellington, New Zealand, the world's southernmost capital city.

Day and night aren't exactly 12 hours long on the day of the equinox because the Earth's atmosphere refracts, or bends, light in an optical illusion that brings more daylight than there really is. Because of this, the date when day and night are of equal length is usually a few days after the autumnal equinox.

Although some people say the autumnal equinox is the "official" start of fall, no administrative or political organization actually designates that.

In fact, though astronomers say summer ends Sept. 22, meteorologists and climatologists say summer ended Aug. 31, the final day of the three hottest months of the year (June, July and August).

If you were looking forward to cooler temperatures this fall, you might be disappointed. Thanks to a combination of El Niño and climate change, there’s a high likelihood for warmer than normal temperatures to continue this fall, said Zach Labe, climate scientist at Climate Central.

"The summer that is just ending was one for the record books, with record ocean heat, the warmest month recorded globally," Labe said. "And extremes like these could be just the beginning."

Worldwide, August was the warmest on record for land and ocean temperatures combined and the August average in the U.S. set records in terms of maximum, average and minimum temperatures, Labe said.

"El Niño is all about redistributing heat," so the heat comes from the ocean and is transferred into the atmosphere, Labe said. That’s why El Niño years often add an additional boost to global temperatures.

Through August, the average temperature in 2026 has been the warmest on record in the contiguous United States, and Arizona, California, Colorado, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah and Wyoming each had their warmest start to the calendar year on record, he said.

Even though we’re likely to hear more and more about warm temperature records being broken, "it’s not really El Niño that is breaking those records," Labe said. "It's human-caused climate change. That's what's driving the long-term trend."

Federal forecasters expect El Niño to peak later this fall and to be one of the strongest El Niño events on record, "but that doesn't always necessarily mean stronger impacts," Labe said. "Every El Niño has its own flavor. Each one is different. And so that's really important to keep in mind."

Doyle Rice and Dinah Voyles Pulver are national correspondents for USA TODAY focusing on weather and climate. Reach them at drice@usatoday.com and dpulver@usatoday.com.

title: Priest prepares to care for 31 children if ICE detains their parents
description: Rev. Vidal Rivas has served at St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church for almost two decades. —Dee...
fullText:
When a mother returned to Maryland earlier this year after four months in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, her children, ages one and four, did not recognize her at first. In her absence, they had lived with Vidal Rivas, an Episcopal priest who had agreed to be their temporary guardian if immigration authorities took her into custody.

Rivas’ wife slept beside the children to soothe them while their mother was gone. When his wife became sick, Rivas took on more of the childcare.

The experience was demanding. But Rivas, 62, stands ready to do the same for 29 other children whose immigrant parents have named him as their standby guardian. Two more families are making similar arrangements with him, he says.

“I feel a lot of responsibility, and a very heavy weight,” says Rivas, who has served at St. Matthews Episcopal Church in suburban Washington for nearly two decades.

Inside the church hangs a sign bearing the same message in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole: “We love migrants.” For Rivas, the words have become a commitment to the families who fear an immigration arrest could suddenly separate them from their children.

Rivas began encouraging families to name him as a standby guardian last year, shortly after President Donald Trump returned to office. Nearly all of the parents are Salvadoran, like him, and have been bracing for the Trump Administration to end Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for roughly 170,000 immigrants from that country.

“It's not easy for parents to know that they could be arrested and their children could be left [in the U.S.] without them,” says Rivas.

Under Maryland law, parents can designate a standby guardian in the event they are arrested by immigration authorities. The designated guardian automatically becomes the child’s legal guardian for six months, with the possibility to extend if approved by a judge. Rivas says some parents have talked to him about contingency plans in case they remain in a detention center for longer.

Maryland was among the first states to revise its guardianship laws to help prevent the children of detained immigrants from entering foster care. During Trump’s first term, state lawmakers passed a law allowing families to name a temporary guardian if detention or deportation separates their family. In July, Massachusetts made a similar change in state law, joining Virginia, New York, California, Nevada, and Washington, D.C. to streamline such arrangements.

After the mother of two young children was released, Rivas and his wife remained close to the family.  “We now feel like the children's grandparents, because we still have a close relationship with her, looking after her and looking after the children,” he says.

Caring for the two children made Rivas acutely aware of the scale of what he has agreed to. If immigration enforcement ramps up in Hyattsville, a small city where more than a third of the population is Hispanic, he could be called upon to care for many children at once.

Such fears have been further exacerbated by the uncertainty surrounding TPS, a program Congress created in 1990 to protect immigrants who cannot safely return to countries affected by armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary conditions. El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS in 1990 due to its civil war, and that protection was renewed in 2001 after the country endured a pair of earthquakes. Since 1990, more than 170,000 Salvadorans have been granted TPS status, becoming one of the largest groups protected by the program.

The Trump administration has recently rolled back TPS protections for more than a dozen other groups—including Haitians, Hondurans, and Nicaraguans—fueling fears that El Salvador could be next.

In early September, hours before the TPS designation for Salvadorans was set to expire, the Department of Homeland Security released a notice that suggested it would remain in place for now. The short notice said Salvadorans under TPS would continue to “retain protection including work authorization,” but added that an announcement on the program’s future “will be made at the appropriate time.”

The statement offered little reassurance. Reports quickly emerged of Salvadorans in Hyattsville and elsewhere losing their jobs amid confusion over their immigration status. Even those still employed worry that the Trump Administration’s reprieve is only temporary.

“Many people have left the church for other cities, and some have returned to their country,” Rivas says. “People are in fear and become insecure.”

Maryland is home to many Salvadorans who fled to the United States in the 1990s or the early 2000s. Around that time, El Salvador was just rebuilding itself from a brutal civil war, before a powerful hurricane and two earthquakes hit the Central American country.

For those who have been in the United States for more than 20 years, returning home may no longer feel like a viable option. More than 27% of El Salvador’s population lives below the national poverty line, according to the World Bank. It also has the highest imprisonment rate in the world, according to data from the World Prison Brief, a database compiled by the Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research (ICPR) at Birkbeck, University of London. President Nayib Bukele has overseen an aggressive crackdown on gang violence as well as critics of his administration. The strategy is credited with reducing the country’s crime rate, but rights groups accuse his government of arbitrary detention and abuses in prison. Last year, Trump sent hundreds of deported Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador’s CECOT, a maximum security jail designated for gang members.

Rivas grew up in El Salvador during another tumultuous era. A military coup in 1979 led to a deadly decade-long civil war between the U.S.-backed Salvadoran government and a left-wing guerrilla group backed by Cuba.

Rivas decided to become a Catholic priest at age 27. He says the military viewed Catholic clergy who advocated for social justice and human rights as communists. He was detained, beaten and hospitalized, he says.

Rivas came to the U.S. in 1998 to work at a Catholic Church in Washington, D.C., where his advocacy work put him at odds with the church’s leadership. He eventually converted to the more liberal Episcopalian Church, and joined St. Matthews in 2008.

As the church’s Hispanic membership has grown, Rivas has felt an increasing responsibility to help parishioners struggling with immigration issues. Watching parents cry as they discussed what might happen to them—and their children—convinced him that he had to do more.

Rivas says the support from the community over his guardian commitments has been overwhelming. Many have donated clothes and toys, and other churches and immigration organizations are also helping parents with standby guardianship arrangements.

If he ultimately takes in more children, he intends to open a bank account in the church’s name to accept donations to cover the costs of childcare. “I know that there are also other churches that are willing to support us,” he says.

Rivas acknowledges that caring for so many children at once would be an enormous challenge. But in the current political environment, he sees it as “a moral obligation.”

“I'm going to keep doing it as much as I can,” he says.

title: Trump's plan to militarize proposed arch raises new concerns
description:
President Donald Trump’s push to convert his planned triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery into a military complex has complicated a required federal review process and raised new legal and safety concerns.
Trump unveiled his new national security rationale Sunday in a post on Truth Social, saying that the 250-foot-tall arch project - which he has framed for nearly a year as a tourist attraction - will now house drones, snipers and ammunition. The president said he was making the change at the request of the U.S. military.
fullText:
President Donald Trump's push to convert his planned triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery into a military complex has complicated a required federal review process and raised new legal and safety concerns.

Trump unveiled his new national security rationale Sunday in a post on Truth Social, saying that the 250-foot-tall arch project - which he has framed for nearly a year as a tourist attraction - will now house drones, snipers and ammunition. The president said he was making the change at the request of the U.S. military.

Critics of the plan saw echoes of Trump's shifting security case for the White House ballroom, which the administration has used to defend that project in court. But while presidents have historically had some leeway to revamp the White House grounds, the arch would stand on federal parkland more than a mile away, where Congress has set stricter rules for construction.

"There is nothing that authorizes or justifies a massive arch, even if Trump tries to disguise it as a military facility," said Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on a House committee that oversees federal parkland. "This is cartoonishly illegal, but he's obviously trying to find a way to do it anyway."

Aviation experts warned Monday that using drones at the planned arch site - Memorial Circle, a roundabout near Reagan National Airport - could pose risks in the airport's crowded airspace.

"Anything you add to the airspace complicates the airspace and increases the operational risk," said Tom Lintner, a former safety official at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

Other military and safety experts have questioned the implications of storing ammunition in the middle of a heavily used traffic circle and whether tourists could still enter the arch as previously planned.

Historic preservationists participating in a required federal review process said they could not move forward until the administration clarifies Trump's plans for the arch. Administration officials last week had asked Washington and Virginia's preservation offices to agree to a memorandum of agreement (MOA) by Monday as part of that process, and they invited other preservationists to participate.

"This MOA is DOA," Charles Birnbaum of the Cultural Landscape Foundation wrote in an email to the administration on Monday. An official for Washington's historic preservation office also wrote in an email that the office needed clarity on Trump's post. Both emails were shared with The Washington Post.

Administration officials have declined to offer further details about Trump's plans to convert the arch to a military complex. They have previously said that they will not begin construction on the arch until they have received "all necessary approvals."

But Trump has pushed his deputies to expedite the arch and other construction projects, particularly in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling on Aug. 31 that let him continue building his ballroom, according to two people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. The ruling did not decide the merits of the case.

Spokespeople for the White House and Pentagon said on Monday that they had no additional information to provide beyond the president's social media post. A defense official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said it was not clear if U.S. Northern Command, which oversees domestic military operations, has been asked to develop any related plans.

Military officials with Joint Task Force-National Capital Region, which oversees military operations to protect D.C., did not respond to requests for comment on Monday. Spokespeople for the Interior Department and the National Park Service also did not respond to questions about the project. The Federal Aviation Administration referred questions to the White House.

Until Sunday, the Trump administration had largely portrayed the arch as a prominent tourist attraction. Architectural plans posted by the National Park Service last month include a "ticket booth," a "family restroom" and other features atypical of any active military complex.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum mentioned that the arch would also offer a "military observation deck" in a social media post earlier this month.

The administration had already faced safety questions, in part because the 250-foot-tall structure would sit directly in National Airport flight paths. Aviation safety there has garnered significant attention since a 2025 collision between an Army helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet near the airport that killed 67 people.

On Friday, the FAA said it had determined that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, including at National Airport. That finding preceded Trump's announcement about drones, whose type and frequency of use remain unclear.

In its final study on the arch, the FAA said the proposed structure should feature "a nonstandard eternal flame" to make it noticeable to pilots. It also said the arch should be continuously floodlighted by searchlight projectors around its base.

Jeff Guzzetti, a former FAA and National Transportation Safety Board accident investigator, said having drones in the flight path of National would worsen the airport's congestion problem.

"Even not knowing how often these things are going to be used, it would certainly increase the risk of a collision with a commercial airliner," Guzzetti said.

Michael McCormick, coordinator of the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said he expected the FAA would need to conduct another study.

"Whatever the drones are, no matter what, the FAA would have to approve their flight because it's civilian airspace," McCormick said. "It cannot be a unilateral decision by the Pentagon."

title: U.S. broadcaster boycott against Trump faced 1st test at ribbon cutting ceremony
description:
The fallout from President Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House continued on Monday, with the news organizations filing a federal lawsuit, other outlets dropping their coverage in protest and the administration launching a live YouTube stream branded “TRUMP TV.”
In response  to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. 
As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.
fullText:
The fallout from President Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House continued on Monday, with the news organizations filing a federal lawsuit, other outlets dropping their coverage in protest and the administration launching a live YouTube stream branded "TRUMP TV."

In response to the ban, four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — refused to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

On Monday night, the White House launched a Trump TV YouTube stream. Branded "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station," the White House said in its description that it would run videos and highlights of "the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." The first video showed Trump's remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social. "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

A hearing was set for Wednesday. Trump indicated in a follow-up Truth Social post that he would appeal any ruling against him.

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced that they would not publish images of Trump's trip on Monday in solidarity with the banned journalists.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on her 2028 plans: ‘Life doesn't wait for you to be ready'

The 36-year-old Congresswoman said she’s not basing her decisions on “deference.” Screenshot
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) says any decisions she makes about her political future won’t be decided by “deference” — and called the years ahead a “very unique political window” as she discussed a possible White House run with The New York Times.

title: ICE hides locations of thousands of detainees with final removal orders
description:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders, an unannounced move that has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice.
ICE removed those detainees from its online detainee locator system on Sept. 15, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the change.
fullText:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders, an unannounced move that has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice.

ICE removed those detainees from its online detainee locator system on Sept. 15, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the change. Several lawyers contacted by The Associated Press confirmed their clients vanished from the system this week, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association warned its members about the situation Friday.

The move represents a stark departure from previous practice and highlights the hardline nature of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, leaving thousands of detainees exceedingly hard to trace and potentially unable to exercise all of their legal options.

The practice, which applies to detainees who have received final orders of removal from an immigration court, could speed deportations by making last-minute legal challenges harder to pursue, immigration lawyers said. Nearly 16,000 people who were arrested and booked into ICE detention in July were subject to final removal orders, more than a third of the overall bookings, according to ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

The practice does not apply to detainees held at a detention facility in Adelanto, California or at temporary holding facilities in Minneapolis, New York City or suburban Chicago, the sources said. Judges have ordered ICE to list detainees in those facilities in the online locator promptly upon their arrival, as part of litigation over their detention practices.

The effort to hide their locations adds to the ways in which the Trump administration has made life harder for detainees and their families as it has increased pressure on them to waive appeals and agree to deportation.

ICE did not publicize the move and in a statement issued to the AP, the agency did not confirm or deny it. The statement said detainees with final removal orders were being prioritized for deportation, even as ICE faces a "historic number of injunctions" from courts stopping individual removals.

As a result of the change, lawyers and relatives lost track of their clients and loved ones without explanation, which is especially concerning because detainees are frequently moved to new facilities before deportation, said Greg Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

"Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don't know where the person might be," he said. "On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship."

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, has argued that people who are subject to final removal orders have received due process. That usually means an immigration judge has ordered their removal after a hearing, including cases when immigrants fail to show up, and the decision was affirmed on appeal or not appealed.

Still, those detainees have options to challenge their detention and removal, including seeking to reopen the case or by bringing what's known as a habeas petition asking a judge to release them on constitutional grounds. Federal judges have granted thousands of rulings ordering that detainees be released or granted bond hearings.

ICE detention facilities held more than 65,000 people as of early July, the most recent available data. Around 30% of them likely have final removal orders, said Michelle Mendez, legal director at the National Immigration Project.

More people have been issued final removal orders after failing to show up for hearings in recent months because the administration's immigration courts have taken steps to make it harder to participate and to reopen such cases, she said.

"To me, it's just another iteration of disappearing people," she said. "Why would we do that in the United States of America? It's something we'd hear about in another country and be concerned about individual rights and due process."

Some with final removal orders also have legal protections against deportation to their countries of origin based on the likelihood they would be tortured or persecuted. Many of them are facing removal to third-party countries where they have no ties and their disappearance in ICE's system will make legal challenges harder, lawyers said.

ICE initiated the online detainee locator system in 2010 to allow relatives, lawyers and the public to search for people in custody. Previously they had to call ICE regional offices or individual facilities to try to track them down.

Many advocates and lawmakers have complained that the system updates too slowly and contains too much inaccurate or missing information, allowing ICE to shield the locations of detainees for days or weeks. Minors, people who have been held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection for less than 48 hours, and detainees who are being transported are not in the system, among others.

But the exclusion of detainees with final removal orders has no apparent parallel, several immigration lawyers said. Atenas Burrola Estrada, a deputy program director with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said that "every single one of our clients who has a final order has disappeared from the locator," including 17 in all as of Monday.

Among those disappeared from the locator system are eight Somali men being detained at the U.S. military base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, according to one of their attorneys, My Khanh Ngo, of the American Civil Liberties Union. She said the change could make it "nearly impossible" for people to challenge their removals in some cases.

"If you can't find your client, don't know what's happening to your client, you can't get that information to the court to stop their removal," she said.

title: Trump tells CNN reporter ahead of U.N. speech, 'you shouldn't be here' amid media ban
description:
President Donald Trump lashed out at CNN‘s Kaitlan Collins before his address the U.N. General Assembly in New York amid the White House ban to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access.
Those three news outlets are suing the president for violating the First Amendment.
Collins asked Trump as he entered the U.
fullText:
President Donald Trump gave his highly anticipated U.N. General Assembly speech Tuesday morning in front of a standing room only crowd.

However, as Trump spoke about the last six months of Iran military strikes, that country's U.N. delegates walked out of the assembly.

Trump told the gathering of world leaders in New York City said that he had a "big decision" coming up on Iran.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump asked.

“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” The president continued: “Do I drive them into hell?”

Trump said he believes Tehran will “make a deal right after the [midterm] election” in November.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are in New York for the annual meeting but didn’t attend Trump’s speech. However, their staff and delegates watched the beginning of Trump's speech then exited the General Assembly 10 minutes into his remarks. Only one Iranian delegate remained in the hall to listen to the U.S. president.

As Trump spoke about Iran, the camera panned to the lone remaining delegate from Iran, who glared stone-faced at the president.

Newsweek reached out to the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump also said in his speech that he's not concerned about the war in Iran hurting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The election “doesn’t even enter my mind” when it comes to Iran, he said.

A new NBC News poll found widespread skepticism toward the conflict, with 62 percent of voters saying the war has not been worth it and 57 percent saying they would be less likely to support candidates who back it. The findings arrive amid growing Republican unease over the war's political costs, particularly in competitive midterm races.

Diesel has risen to a record $6.50 amid ongoing supply constraints from the Iran war and other global pressures, exposing a significant political vulnerability for the GOP.

Still, Trump said he’s not concerned with politics.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said of Iran. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide … and I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years.”

President Trump lashed out at CNN's Kaitlan Collins before his address the U.N. General Assembly in New York amid the White House ban to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access.

Those three news outlets are suing the president for violating the First Amendment.

Collins asked Trump as he entered the U.N. building, "Two thirds of Americans don't think the U.S. is winning the war with Iran. When will it end?"

Arriving with First Lady Melania Trump, Trump brushed aside the question and told Collins: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me."

After Trump's comments, Collins said on CNN that the network "never said we were not going to cover the president" and vowed that CNN would continue reporting on him despite the White House's efforts to restrict its access. She noted that the network was covering the president from the United Nations under U.N. credentials while the legal fight over White House access continues.

This is a breaking news article. Updates to follow.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

title: Former NFL team physician breaks down Jayden Daniels' options after elbow injury
description: Following quarterback Jayden Daniels' second left elbow dislocation, he could wear a brace for the season and miss less time or have surgery.
fullText:
With Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels dislocating his left elbow again in Washington's Week 2 loss to the Dallas Cowboys, the Commanders have options for what to do next, according to former NFL team physician Dr. David J. Chao.

Jayden Daniels could return sooner than expected with an elbow brace, but he’ll likely need it for the rest of the season.

Why surgery could still be considered, and why not operating after the first dislocation wasn’t a mistake. pic.twitter.com/4lhBk2dmuk

Essentially, Chao says Daniels could return sooner than expected if he is willing to wear an elbow brace for the rest of the season. That is because he is right-handed and the injury is to his left elbow, so he can still throw the ball. Daniels would probably have to be less aggressive running the ball to minimize contact on the elbow.

Chao also presents the possibility that Daniels could opt for surgery to repair his elbow to prevent future issues with the elbow. Given this is the second time Daniels has dislocated this elbow — he also aggravated it when he returned last season — it would not be surprising if this is the choice he ultimately went with. If he opts for surgery, he would miss the remainder of the season, but should be fully healthy for the offseason program next spring. It would be the second season in a row Daniels would miss significant time due to injury.

This would also probably mean another year Washington does not make the playoffs. They are already in a hole after losing their second division game of the season and face an uphill battle in their third game of the year against the Seattle Seahawks, the defending Super Bowl champions.

This article originally appeared on Commanders Wire: Former NFL team physician breaks down Jayden Daniels' options after elbow injury

title: Fantasy football Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: 16 players to start or sit in Week 3
description: Injuries to Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels will create some tough start 'em, sit 'em decisions for fantasy managers in Week 3.
fullText:
If Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season was kind to fantasy football managers, Week 2 was brutal.

After a high-scoring start to the 2026 campaign, offensive results sagged a bit in Week 2. A handful of injuries to key fantasy producers made matters worse, most notably Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams and Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels.

Those injuries, plus a lack of production from some expected stars, will force fantasy football managers into some difficult start 'em, sit 'em decisions in Week 3.

Of course, it's still important not to overreact. It's early in the season, and some of these players will bounce back. But if you're looking to shake things up, it's fine to make a bold lineup decision or two to spark your squad.

Who can you start and sit in fantasy football for Week 3 of the 2026 NFL season? USA TODAY Sports outlines eight players to start and eight to sit:

Patrick Mahomes, Kansas City Chiefs (at Miami Dolphins)

Mahomes was viewed as a risky fantasy pick ahead of the 2026 NFL season after returning from a torn ACL that prematurely ended his 2025 campaign. He has quelled those concerns by logging three total touchdowns in each of his first two games while showing off more explosive, down-the-field playmaking ability after reuniting with Eric Bieniemy. The Dolphins have allowed the seventh-most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to quarterbacks and have a thin defense that Mahomes should easily exploit.

Tyler Shough, New Orleans Saints (vs. Las Vegas Raiders)

Through two weeks, Shough leads the NFL in passing yards with 662 and is one of just two quarterbacks to attempt 90 passes in his first two games. The Saints haven't been able to run the ball much yet, so Kellen Moore may keep relying on his second-year quarterback to carry New Orleans' offense. The Raiders have started better-than-expected on defense and have only allowed two touchdowns to quarterbacks, but Shough nonetheless has QB1 upside because of his volume.

TreVeyon Henderson, New England Patriots (at Jacksonville Jaguars)

Henderson missed Week 1 with an ankle injury but out-touched Rhamondre Stevenson 16-7 against the Steelers. Stevenson also lost a fumble, a long-term issue of his, so it stands to reason that Henderson will remain the backfield leader for now. The Jaguars have been solid against running backs, but it may take only one play for the speedy Henderson to become a worthwhile RB2.

Quinshon Judkins, Cleveland Browns (vs. Carolina Panthers)

Is it fun to back a guy averaging 2.3 yards per carry? No, but this is easily Judkins' best matchup of the season. The Panthers have allowed a league-high 347 rushing yards to running backs and just saw Falcons backup Brian Robinson Jr. total 51 yards on 11 carries against them. Expect Judkins to have his best day of the season and maybe find the end zone.

Adonai Mitchell, New York Jets (at Detroit Lions)

Mitchell has already established a rapport with Geno Smith, garnering a team-high 15 targets over the Jets' first two games. Now he faces a Lions team missing its top three safeties and having surrendered a league-high 437 receiving yards to wideouts to start the season. That should make Mitchell a potential boom candidate and WR2.

Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts (vs. Houston Texans)

Houston's defense is well-regarded, but it has been porous to open the 2026 NFL season. It has allowed the third-most FPPG to wide receivers thus far, so Downs – who will be the Colts' No. 1 receiver if Alec Pierce (heel) is out – could enjoy a quality outing in what might be another high-scoring Colts game.

Dalton Schultz, Houston Texans (at Indianapolis Colts)

The Colts just got shredded in prime-time by 36-year-old Travis Kelce. Schultz just caught 12 passes for 140 yards against the Bengals. He should remain a quality security blanket for C.J. Stroud and will be well-positioned to take advantage of a favorable matchup.

Carolina Panthers (at Cleveland Browns)

The Panthers just beat up on a Falcons team starting Cooper Rush at quarterback. Now they face Deshaun Watson, who is coming off a good game against the Buccaneers but hasn't performed well in Cleveland. If Devin Lloyd can have another big name, expect Carolina to thrive in this spot.

Justin Herbert, Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Buffalo Bills)

Did the Bills just allow Stroud and Jared Goff to post massive games against them? Yes. But can you really trust Herbert after he averaged 200.5 passing yards, two total touchdowns and three interceptions against the Cardinals and Raiders? It's not advisable, especially since Greg Rousseau and Deone Walker should be able to wreak havoc against a beleaguered Chargers offensive line.

Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. New England Patriots)

The Patriots have allowed a league-low 8 points per game through two weeks of the 2026 NFL season. Granted, Drew Lock and Aaron Rodgers were the primary quarterbacks taking snaps in those contests, but New England's defense still looks strong. Don't be surprised if Lawrence, who failed to log a touchdown against the Broncos in Week 2, struggles in this matchup.

MarShawn Lloyd, Green Bay Packers (at Atlanta Falcons)

Lloyd is averaging just 3 yards per carry and is splitting touches with Kaleb Johnson and Chris Brooks. He could be a TD-dependent flex play, but it's too risky to start him against a Falcons defense that has allowed the seventh-fewest FPPG to RBs this season.

Jadarian Price, Seattle Seahawks (at Washington Commanders)

Price gets a good matchup against the Commanders, but it's hard to trust him as anything more than a speculative flex. Emanuel Wilson seems like Seattle's preferred goal-line option while George Holani is also mixing into the running back rotation. Add in that Price fumbled against the Cardinals and left early with an injury, and fantasy managers are probably better off sitting him until he carves out a larger, more consistent role.

Stefon Diggs, Washington Commanders (vs. Seattle Seahawks)

Three of Diggs' nine catches to open the 2026 NFL season have gone for touchdowns, but he is facing a brutal matchup against the Seahawks in Week 3. Seattle is allowing the fewest FPPG to receivers this season and Diggs will have to do damage with backup quarterback Marcus Mariota playing in place of the injured Daniels. That doesn't seem like a recipe for success.

Rome Odunze, Chicago Bears (vs. Philadelphia Eagles)

Odunze is in a similar boat to Diggs. Williams may not play in Week 3 because of a hamstring injury, in which case Tyson Bagent would be tasked with leading Chicago's offense. Bagent doesn't have the same arm strength as Odunze, so that may make it tough for the veteran receiver – who has a 19.57 average depth of target (ADOT), per Sumer Sports – to make the big plays needed to emerge as a quality fantasy asset.

Colston Loveland, Chicago Bears (vs. Philadelphia Eagles)

Yes, we are recommending to sit multiple Bears pass-catching weapons. The Eagles have only allowed six catches and 42 yards to tight ends thus far in 2026 and Loveland has just one catch for three yards across his first two games. Perhaps playing with Bagent will spark him, but more likely, his slow start will continue.

Minnesota Vikings (at Tampa Bay Buccaneers)

The good news for the Buccaneers? Baker Mayfield has performed well against the blitz, which could set him up for success against Brian Flores' defense. The bad news? He has been sacked seven times and has turned the ball over four times in his first two games. Those turnover issues should make Minnesota's defense a high-floor play, even if Mayfield is able to beat the blitz. He's bound to make a mistake at some point.

title: Tony White takes responsibility for FSU defense
description: Defensive coordinator Tony White says he is to blame for Florida State's defensive struggles against Alabama.
fullText:
Florida State's defense has faced mounting scrutiny through the first three games of the season, and defensive coordinator Tony White made it clear Monday that he believes much of the responsibility falls on him.

The Seminoles surrendered 567 yards in Saturday's loss to Alabama, allowing the Crimson Tide to score on nine consecutive possessions after a promising start defensively. Florida State opened the game by forcing five straight third-down stops, but once Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell found his rhythm in the second half, the Seminoles had no answers.

White said the collapse reminded him of last season's loss to Virginia, when Florida State was unable to make a critical stop late in the game, eventually forcing overtime and suffering its first defeat of the season.

"It starts with me first," White said.

"I mean, that's my fault. I should've stayed aggressive, should've stayed attacking. Sometimes when you get hit on a play or something, you kind of look at the call and say, 'OK, that didn't work, so let me not call that.' We were calling that all in the first half. They made a play. Guess what? Call it again on the next play. And we hit it again for one or two yards. So I just got to be really critical of myself and make sure that the guys who were doing well keep having confidence in that and let them go play."

More: Mike Norvell: FSU RB Samuel Singleton Jr. FSU RB out for extended time

White repeatedly pointed to his own play-calling decisions while reflecting on what went wrong against Alabama. After coming close to upsetting the eighth-ranked Crimson Tide for a second consecutive season, Florida State could not maintain its early defensive momentum.

The defensive struggles have been evident throughout the opening three games. The Seminoles enter this week with a 1-2 record and have allowed 1,471 total yards and 94 points.

Florida State generated four turnovers in its loss to SMU, but the defense failed to force a takeaway against Alabama. The Seminoles also rank 117th nationally in pressure rate, a concerning statistic for a unit built around White's aggressive philosophy.

"It was me," White said. "I'm always going to stand up in here and tell you the truth. It was me. I shouldn't have stayed aggressive, stayed attacking. The guys were on fire. They were humming, chasing ghosts up there.

"There were some defenses that were really good, and we gave up a big play, and I didn't even call it again because I didn't even see the defensive efficiency deal on there. So I should have called it about 10 more times. I need to be better at that and let those guys play."

More: Final: Alabama extends Seminoles' woes, FSU tumbles 50-36

Despite the disappointing performance, White praised his defense's effort in one of college football's toughest environments at Bryant-Denny Stadium.

He highlighted several young contributors, including defensive linemen Kevin "JuJu" Wynn and Darryll Desir, for making positive impressions against Alabama.

While White openly accepted responsibility for the breakdowns against the Crimson Tide, he said the focus now shifts to correcting mistakes and restoring confidence within the unit. The team, which also took accountability as White fully disclosed in their team meeting, is still all in.

Florida State will have an opportunity to do just that Saturday when it hosts Central Arkansas at 3 p.m. at Doak Campbell Stadium. For White and the Seminoles, the challenge is straightforward: learn from a costly collapse and rediscover the aggressive identity that helped make the defense successful in the first place.

"In terms of confidence, no, it's had nothing to do with confidence. It's all about the process, White said.

"As you look at what works, what doesn't, and really it's the players. You look at them and how they believe, right? You don't play that hard and not believe in what you're doing and not having an answer for things, you know? Like you don't play that hard and not trust the coaches, not trust the staff, not trust the process that we have. So they believe, they see it."

White's accountability may not erase the frustration of Florida State's defensive collapse against Alabama, but it offers a clear starting point as the Seminoles look to reverse their early-season struggles. With conference play looming and a defense searching for consistency, Florida State has little time to dwell on missed opportunities. The response against Central Arkansas could provide an early indication of whether White's self-assessment leads to the defensive turnaround the Seminoles desperately need.

title: These 5 Mets prospects can make the biggest impact in 2027 season
description: With the minor league season coming to a close, and a retooled Mets system, here are the contenders for a call-up at the end of 2026.
fullText:
The Minor League Baseball regular season came to a close on Sunday, and much like the Mets, neither of the team's top two affiliates was able to secure a playoff spot.

That's not to say that neither had success. In the second half, Triple-A Syracuse finished one and a half games back of Rochester for the second-half title in the International League's East Division.

After Double-A Binghamton was 15 games under .500 in the first half of the Eastern League season, they were .500 at 34-34 in the second half.

An infusion of talent came to the Mets system at Major League Baseball's Aug. 3 trade deadline when the club sent away eight major league players and retooled their farm system. It provided the Mets' front office with an arsenal of young potential that can be used to fill in the voids on the major league roster or bring in other proven assets for 2027 season.

As that season came to a close, here are the five Mets prospects who could see a major league opportunity in 2026:

The 21-year-old was the top prospect acquired by the Mets at the deadline in the deal that sent Clay Holmes and Tyrone Taylor to the Cubs. A month and a half later, the Mets had elevated Rojas to Triple-A Syracuse after he slashed .280/.336/.593 with nine home runs, 29 RBI and 24 runs in 29 games in Binghamton. R

ojas collected eight hits, including three home runs, in six games in Syracuse.

As Zac Thornton pitched his way into serious contention for a 2027 rotation spot, a path could be seen for Santucci, who was named the Mets' Minor League Pitcher of the Year this season. Santucci is not a hard thrower, but he has gotten more effective as his control has strengthened and his changeup and curveball have improved.

After posting a 3-7 record with a 3.57 ERA and 1.25 WHIP with 120 strikeouts in Double-A Binghamton, Santucci made eight starts in Syracuse, where he allowed 20 earned runs in 34⅓ innings.

At one time, it appeared as though Wenninger was headed toward a major league debut in the 2026 season, but the 24-year-old's control wavered in his first full season in Triple A. The stuff is there, with a mid-90s fastball and splitter off that offering but he walked 68 batters in 115 innings this season and his way to a 4.54 ERA.

Wenninger's potential has him checking in as the Mets' top right-handed pitching prospect at the end of this season.

The 23-year-old infielder was part of a three-prospect package that sent Freddy Peralta to the AL East-leading Rays. The former 2024 second-round pick, whose best tool is his hitting ability, has risen to the Mets' No. 10 prospect rank.

The left-handed hitting Pitrie was 15-for-40 (.375) with seven runs and seven RBI in Double-A Binghamton before moving up to Syracuse two weeks after the deadline. In his first Triple-A action, Pitrie slashed .260/.357/.370 with five extra-base hits, including one home run, five RBI and nine runs in 20 games.

Clifford's quest to reach the big leagues might not come with the Mets, but if he is not added to the Mets' 40-man roster before December, he would be opened up to the Rule 5 Draft.

In his first full season in Triple-A Syracuse, Clifford struck out 174 times in 115 games. The power tool is still there. He hit 18 home runs and added 17 doubles with 56 RBI and 59 runs, but his feast-or-famine reality makes him more of a play on potential than reality right now.

title: NFL analyst gives Panthers perfect grade for Week 2 win
description: The Panthers were at the top of the class for Week 2.
fullText:
It's only been two games, but the Carolina Panthers look more potent than they have in a decade as they move into Week 3 of the 2026 season.

The offense has been particularly impressive so far, averaging 35.5 points per game, second in the NFL only behind 2024 Most Valuable Player Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. They also rank fifth in yardage at 409.0 per contest.

Defensively, there's definitely room for improvement. However, the Panthers have also proven they have radically upgraded at both linebacker spots and are getting solid contributions on the back end from their rookie class already.

As a bonus, the Panthers appear to have found another weapon on special teams in the form of wide receiver Jalen Coker—who took his first career punt return for 36 yards in Sunday's 34-3 win.

Oh, and according to CBS Sports, the Panthers deserve an 'A+' grade for that Week 2 demolishing of the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. John Breech writes:

After giving up 59 points in Week 1, this was the kind of rebound game that the Panthers needed. They were nearly flawless in all three phases of the game. The defense took advantage of a struggling Falcons offense by forcing four turnovers, including a pick-six from Devin Lloyd. The player of the game was Bryce Young (287 passing yards and three touchdowns), who looked like a star for the second straight week. Right now, it's hard to tell if Young has truly taken the next step or if he's taken advantage of two bad defenses, but whatever the case may be, he's been playing at a high level and if this is how he's going to play all season, then the Panthers will have a good shot of repeating as NFC South champs.

The Panthers have a solid chance of entering their Week 5 bye at 3-1. Week 3 will see them travel to take on the Cleveland Browns and Week 4 will play host to a Sunday nighter against a vulnerable Detroit Lions defense.

title: How did Ohio State's Ryan Day help Kevin McGuff land Sydney Mobley?
description: Sydney Mobley is talented enough on her own to earn a scholarship offer from Ohio State, but a phone call with Ryan Day helped get the process going.
fullText:
Hey. When you get a minute, give me a call.

It wasn't just the message that got the attention of Ohio State women's basketball coach Kevin McGuff – it was the sender. When the text message from Buckeyes football coach Ryan Day reached his cell phone roughly six years ago, McGuff made more than a minute and gave Day a call.

What happened next led to McGuff landing Ohio's 2026 Ms. Basketball a year early. Sydney Mobley, who is a freshman on this year's Ohio State team, was in sixth grade when she turned a few heads at a recreation center in Columbus.

It turned out that Day's father-in-law, Stan Spirou, was also in the gym alongside Day's son, RJ.

"He said, 'There's a girl out here who is crushing people at the rec center,' and she was in like the sixth grade at that time," McGuff said Sept. 21, about an hour before his team's first official practice of the season. "I tracked down some information after that and that's how we started recruiting her."

Now listed at 6-foot-2, Mobley capped a three-year prep career by averaging 20.3 points, 9.6 rebounds, 2.5 steals, 2.3 assists and 1.5 blocks at Big Walnut while earning first-team all-state honors for the third consecutive year. A five-star prospect in the 2027 class, according to the 247Sports.com composite, she reclassified, graduated early, joined Ohio State at the end of the summer and is now preparing for her first collegiate season with the school that offered her a scholarship before she even got to high school.

McGuff said she will face an acclimation period as she gets used to playing at a higher level but that Mobley is expected to be a contributor this season. And for that, he owes at least a little bit of thanks to Ohio State's football coach.

"He has mentioned maybe being our recruiting coordinator at some point," McGuff said with a smile. "He's probably got plenty of national championships and games to win still in football, but he may have a secondary career in recruiting for Ohio State women's basketball."

title: What we know about Giants injuries, including Jaxson Dart and Andrew Thomas
description: Jaxson Dart. Andrew Thomas. Malik Nabers. Brian Burns. Losing one to injury is tough enough for Giants.
fullText:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. - Behind the scenes, the New York Giants would have signed for this reality with two primetime games against one opponent that was a prohibitive Super Bowl favorite and another viewed as a legitimate contender.

They are 1-1, and as much as Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams was hard to stomach at times, especially with four franchise cornerstones having left the game due to injury, the season has just begun.

The NFL is a league of extremes, of course. One week the Giants beat the Cowboys in the best atmosphere at MetLife Stadium in more than a decade, and the challenge is about refusing to be complacent.

Now, after falling to the Rams, the Giants' resolve is going to be tested just the same.

"This is a test for everybody," outside linebacker Brian Burns said. "You know, obviously coming off a huge win with Dallas, you know, this is a little piece of humble pie just the way the game went. Nobody should be happy how stuff played out. But all in all, it's not gonna define us. We just gotta get back to work, get back in the win column and that's something I feel like we're gonna do."

The questions that remain center on those injuries to quarterback Jaxson Dart, Burns, left tackle Andrew Thomas and wide receiver Malik Nabers. Losing one to injury in a game is tough enough for the Giants. All four?

It's a Big Blue nightmare. So what's next and here's what we know about the status of those players?

John Harbaugh says the Giants will know more about Dart's knee injury after tests on Tuesday. The initial hope for the team leaving the stadium for the overnight flight back home to New Jersey is that Dart suffered an MCL sprain, a source confirmed to NorthJersey.com and The Record. An MRI will tell the full story, however, but that's better news than what was feared on first look when Dart's left knee collided with the Rams' Josaiah Stewart.

Dart did not speak to reporters in the locker room after the game. If testing shows no additional damage, a typical timetable for an MRI sprain is 2-4 weeks. Dart could return sooner, of course, but for now, the expectation would be that Jameis Winston would start Sunday against the Tennessee Titans at MetLife Stadium if the former is unavailable.

Thomas' groin injury might be the most concerning, given what his presence means to the offensive line. He was on the ground laboring badly following the final two plays for the Giants. With a short week, the Giants could turn to either rookie J.C. Davis or more likely second-year pro Marcus Mbow to fill in for Thomas at left tackle against the Titans.

Nabers said his shoulder popped out after Rams corner Trent McDuffie took a swipe at the football in coverage and raked his right arm. The Giants' No. 1 receiver will undergo further testing, but the hope is that there is no further damage, considering he returned to the game and played to the final whistle.

Burns had his left ankle rolled up late in the fourth quarter and he could barely put any pressure on it. The cart came for Burns after he made his way to the bench, but the Giants' Pro Bowler refused and walked back to the locker room with some assistance.

After the game, Harbaugh said Burns suffered a low ankle sprain. It will be interesting to see how quickly the swelling goes down and the stiffness is alleviated, but considering Burns has played through ankle sprains before - he did so for most of his first season here with the Giants - it'd be hard to count against him being back soon, maybe as early as next week. If not, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux would be in the starting lineup in Burns' absence.

title: Cam Ward earns high marks despite Tennessee Titans loss
description: Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward earned a B grade after a strong performance in a narrow loss to the Philadelphia Eagles.
fullText:
The Tennessee Titans suffered a heartbreaking Week 2 loss, falling 24-20 to the Philadelphia Eagles in a highly competitive matchup.

While there are no moral victories in the NFL, the game was a giant step forward for the Titans, who looked completely overmatched by the New York Jets in Week 1. It was also a solid step forward for the offense and Cam Ward, who used balance and a few explosive plays to put them in a position to win.

So, how did his performance grade out? Brent Soblesky of Bleacher Report was impressed and gave him a positive critique.

Score: 24-20 loss vs. Philadelphia Eagles

Stat Line: 13 of 20 for 183 yards and two rushing touchdowns

Cam Ward's performance in Week 1 caused plenty of doubters to enter the public sphere and question whether he's going to be a franchise quarterback. The 2025 No. 1 overall draft pick responded with a strong outing against the Philadelphia Eagles. Though the Tennessee Titans couldn't hold their fourth-quarter lead and ultimately lost the contest.

In recent weeks, Ward has taken some much-deserved heat, although none of the issues were on him. But as the face of the franchise and a former first-overall pick, he needs to become more consistent and start taking control. Sunday was a positive step, but there is still a lot more room to grow.

title: USC women's golf sets single-round scoring record at Golfweek Red Sky Classic
description: The USC women's golf team set a new single-round scoring record Monday at the Golfweek Red Sky Classic in Colorado.
fullText:
WOLCOTT, CO — The Southern California women's golf team likes playing in the Rocky Mountains.

A year after setting the single-round and tournament scoring records at the Golfweek Red Sky Classic, the Trojans once again had a record-setting performance Monday in the opening round at Red Sky Golf Club's Fazio Course. USC set the single-round scoring record, shooting 22-under 266, one shot better than it carded in the final round last year of its victory. USC has an 11-shot lead over Miami heading to Tuesday's second round.

Junior Jasmine Koo, who finished as co-medalist a year ago, signed for 7-under 65 on Monday. Freshman Kaili Xiao, making her collegiate debut, also signed for 65 after a back-nine 30. Kylie Chong, who shared co-medalist honors with Koo in 2025, got in at 6-under 66.

More: Golfweek Red Sky Classic scores

Xiao's 65 is believed to be the best debut round by a freshman in school history. It's also the lowest round in school history, besting last year's mark.

Sophomore Sarah Hammett also had a bogey-free 70 as the final counting score.

Cameron Jourdan is an assistant editor of Golfweek, covering college and amateur golf, the PGA Tour and plenty more. Follow Cameron on X/Twitter (@Cam_Jourdan) or Instagram (@GolfweekJourdan).

title: 3 new teams join New Jersey Super 25 rankings after upset-filled week
description: After an upset-filled week of the high school football season, three new teams joined the latest New Jersey Super 25 rankings.
fullText:
After an upset-filled week of the high school football season, three new teams joined the New Jersey Super 25 rankings.

West Orange debuts at No. 23 after becoming the first public school to beat Shabazz in a regular-season game in nearly two years. Ramapo, which beat West Orange earlier this season, moved into the rankings at No. 18. Brick Memorial slides in at No. 25 after upsetting previously-ranked Toms River North.

There's also a new team in the No. 2 spot as undefeated St. Augustine moves up after previous No. 2 St. Peter's Prep was beaten by Bergen Catholic.

Every week, voters from across USA TODAY NETWORK New Jersey rank the Top 25 teams in the state. The rankings are posted every Tuesday morning.

This week, there are three matchups between ranked teams:

No. 3 St. Joseph (Montvale) at No. 1 Don Bosco

No. 2 St. Augustine at No. 17 Millville

No. 11 Wayne Hills at No. 5 Old Tappan

Senior running back Colin Schoellkopf ran for a career-high 212 yards and two TDs as the Mustangs defeated then-No. 25 Toms River North, 24-14. Senior Shawn Fowler returned a punt 75 yards for a TD and senior Jack Marotta booted a 24-yard field goal in the win.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Point Pleasant Borough (2-2)

Nosym Brown's 18-yard touchdown catch from Kariem Coston were the only points the Bulldogs could manage in a 13-6 loss to West Orange on Sept. 18. Shabazz had not lost a regular-season game to a public-school opponent since October 2024.

Next game: Sept. 26 at Bayonne (3-1)

Quarterback Daniel Lewis rushed for 118 yards and found Sydney Padilla for a 28-yard touchdown pass as the Mountaineers defeated then-No. 6 Shabazz, 13-6, on Sept. 18. Since a one-point loss to Ramapo on Aug. 27, West Orange has won three straight games and allowed six total points.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. East Orange (2-1)

Junior quarterback Brady Williams continued his early-season tear as he went 23-for-34 for a career-high 331 yards in the Bulldogs' 35-12 win over Wall. Williams threw TD passes of 13 yards to senior Michael Capra, 24 yards to senior Jason Tucker and 83 yards to senior Cole Spoonire, and ran for 89 yards with TD runs of 26 and 9 yards. Senior Jackson Wile booted a 25-yard field goal in the win.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Manalapan (2-2)

Deacon Frayne's 1-yard touchdown run in the final seconds of regulation pushed West Morris to a 22-14 win over Roxbury. The winning score was set up by a 37-yard pass from Matt Zisa to Julian Healy down to the 1-yard line. The victory was the 220th for coach Kevin Hennelly, tying him with legendary former coach Pete Piccirillo for the school record.

Next game: Sept. 26 at Chatham (2-2)

The Stateliners earned their first New Jersey win by topping Hillsborough, 35-7. Phillipsburg opened a 35-0 lead at halftime as Shane Moore rushed for 120 yards and three scores, and Vincent Berger added a pair of rushing TDs.

Next game: Sept. 26 at St. Joseph (Metuchen) (2-1)

Tyler Castillo's 56-yard touchdown pass from Justin Reed in the fourth quarter made the difference in the Marauders' 21-14 win over Chatham. Senior Malcolm Gilyard rushed for 139 yards and two touchdowns in the victory.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Morris Knolls (3-1)

The Green Raiders took to the air in a 34-20 win at Union City. Sophomore Luke Magerko threw for 258 yards, with first-quarter TD passes of 14 yards to senior Hunter Randolph and 73 yards to senior Tyler Hayward for a 13-0 lead. Junior Joey Gorga ran for two TDs and senior Jack Schneider's 41-yard pick-six made it 34-6.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Passaic Tech (2-2)

Senior Reggie Holley rushed for two touchdowns and caught a pass for a third score as the Thunderbolts returned to the win column with a 30-19 triumph at Kingsway. Senior Robbie O'Connor threw for two scores, raising his career total to 54, one shy of the program record held by Nate Robbins set in 2021. Millville overcame a first-quarter deficit to earn the road win.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. St. Augustine (4-0)

The Panthers returned to the field after a bye week and delivered a 32-8 victory at previously-unbeaten Ocean City. Roman Duckett and Jayden Boyce each ran for a pair of touchdowns as Camden produced a season-high 32 points and rushed for 246 yards and five TDs.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Cedar Creek (0-4)

Senior quarterback Charlie Foulke made an impressive debut with his new team, completing 21 of 32 passes for 300 yards and four touchdowns, and rushing for a fifth score. Foulke had to sit out the first three games following his transfer from Philadelphia's St. Joseph Prep, where he was regarded as one of the top QBs in the Keystone State. The Syracuse commit threw a pair of TD passes to Oregon commit Xavier Sabb.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Holy Spirit (1-3)

After outscoring opponents 114-13 across the first three weeks, the Eagles ran into a buzzsaw during a 42-14 loss at St. Augustine. Winslow had its 14-game winning streak snapped as it surrendered 28 unanswered points in the road contest. The Eagles were held to 109 yards of total offense and turned the football over three times in the loss.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Atlantic City (1-3)

The Paladins lost at home to top-ranked Don Bosco, 35-9. Senior Chukwuma Odoh rushed for 75 yards, including a 2-yard TD. Sophomore Walker Snee threw for 73 yards and passed for 83 yards. Junior Rowan Martin threw for 53 yards. Junior Harry Jones opened the scoring in the first quarter on a 32-yard field goal.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Hun (2-1)

Make it 18 wins in a row for the Minutemen after they traveled to Atlantic City and returned home with a 21-19 victory. Township rolled out to a 21-0 lead in the first half on a pair of TD runs by Cody Halicks and a 60-yard TD reception by Isaac Parra from Danny Carter. The Minutemen stopped a two-point conversion in the fourth quarter to preserve the win.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Kingsway (0-4)

The Patriots defeated host Nutley, 35-14, after leading 28-0 at halftime. Senior James Wolf passed for 131 yards and two TDs. Junior Ethan Zacharski caught a 46-yard TD pass and ran for a 29-yard score. Junior CJ Puglisi rushed for 89 yards and a TD, and senior Evan Rapoport ran for 77 yards and a score.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Old Tappan (3-0)

The Red Devils surrendered their first points of the season, but remained red-hot with a 36-6 victory over Shawnee in a battle of unbeatens. Junior quarterback Zach Merhar threw five touchdown passes for the second time in three weeks. He connected with Mikey McQueen, a Syracuse commit, and Dre Byrdsong for a pair of touchdowns apiece and a 54-yard strike to Malcolm Harrison. RV has outscored its opponents 134-6 this season.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Cherokee (1-3)

Senior running back Alex Staten ran for 70 yards and three touchdowns in the Griffins' 35-0 win over Jackson Township. Sophomore Carmelo Foendoe ran for a score, and senior quarterback Kahden Davis went 16-for-22 for 217 yards with a 19-yard TD pass to sophomore Torrence Turner in the win.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Southern (4-0)

Senior running back Jack Bickerton ran for three TDs in the Caseys' 45-23 win over Manalapan. Sophomore quarterback Rahmir Rivera threw TD passes to juniors Jason Berecsky and Ethan Kennedy. Sophomore Simon Picinich booted a 48-yard field goal.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Holmdel (3-1)

The Spartans couldn't run the ball and committed too many critical turnovers in a 42-7 home loss to St. Joseph (Montvale). Junior Frank Morano passed for 182 yards, including a 65-yard score to senior Sean Nevers in the first quarter to cut the deficit to 14-7. Nevers ran for a team-high 34 yards.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Delbarton (2-1)

The Marauders gave up too many yards on the ground – 268 – in a 33-16 home loss to then-No. 7 Bergen Catholic. Senior Bryant Isaac threw for 149 yards, with TD passes of 12 and 6 yards to senior Ty'ire Clark. Junior Bradley Abraham's 32-yard field goal in the second quarter trimmed the deficit to 14-10.

Next game: Oct. 1 vs. Seton Hall Prep (2-2)

The Golden Knights scored the first five TDs in a 35-13 win over visiting River Dell. Senior Nick Blanchard scored on first-quarter runs of 13 and 1 yard for a 14-0 lead. Senior Zach Miceli threw second-quarter scores of 27 yards to senior Leo Etter and 25 yards to senior Shane Small. Senior Julius Lai ran for the final score.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. Wayne Hills (4-0)

The Crusaders registered more than 400 total yards in a 33-16 win at then-No. 2 St. Peter's Prep. Senior Bryan Porter rushed for 154 yards and a TD, and senior Nicholas Mauro ran for 83 yards and two scores. Junior Trey Tagliaferri passed for 134 yards, with a 3-yard TD to senior Anthony Willis putting them ahead to stay, 14-7.

Next game: Oct. 3 vs. Don Bosco (4-0)

The Green Knights returned two interceptions for TDs in a 42-7 victory at DePaul. Junior Tahj Gray had a 15-yard pick-six for a 14-0 lead, and junior Sean Guy closed the scoring on a 35-yard return. Freshman William Mitchell threw for 150 yards, with TD passes to senior Stalin Knowlden and junior Vincent Russo.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Don Bosco (4-0)

Senior Roman Coney, a Cincinnati commit, rushed 28 times for 248 yards and five touchdowns as the Hermits earned a 42-14 home victory over Winslow. The Hermits piled up 312 yards on the ground and scored 35 unanswered points. Coney accounted for St. Augustine's final five touchdowns on runs of 70, 16, 12, 26 and 12 yards.

Next game: Sept. 25 at Millville (2-1)

The Ironmen rode a balanced attack and more than 300 total yards to a 35-9 road win Sept. 18 at then-No. 11 Paramus Catholic. Junior Ca'Si Thomas ran for 120 yards and three TDs. Junior Carson Schoen threw for 165 yards, including a 19-yard score to senior Isaiah Alvarez. Senior Mikahi Allen had 10 tackles, including three sacks.

Next game: Sept. 25 vs. St. Joseph (Montvale) (2-2)
