title: The rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market?
description:
People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis
A December 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”.
fullText:
People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis

A December 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”. Progress indeed.

Nearly six decades on, electric toothbrushes can do a lot more than merely jiggle, offering multiple speeds and movement sensors for real-time tracking of where you’ve brushed – some even promise gum-massage or tongue-cleaning modes. Prices range from about £25 for a basic Oral B model to £599.99 for a Philips Sonicare model that gives “smart coverage feedback”. The latest super-toothbrush – a mere £419.99 – features a camera and a built-in water jet to clean between teeth, using AI to identify gaps. Created by Dyson, it’s still, essentially, a stick with a brush on the end (although there is another toothbrush on the market that’s shaped like a mouthguard, with individual brushes, that claims to clean your teeth in 20 seconds).

In the UK, 59% of adults use an electric toothbrush and sales, including replacement heads, reached £361m in the last year, according to market intelligence company Mintel. Any product launch by Dyson – still associated with reinventing the vacuum cleaner – feels like something of an event, so its incursion into oral health does feel significant, says Rachel Bairsto, the head of museum services at the British Dental Association. “We’re seeing more and more expensive toothbrushes,” she says. “Expensive toothpaste as well.”

These highly designed everyday objects have become symbols of affluence. “If you see a picture of a swanky bathroom, it will definitely have plug sockets for some kind of rechargeable electric toothbrush,” says Bairsto. “Whereas I’ve tried to look through the archives to find pictures of bathrooms with toothbrushes in them, and I can’t. Was everybody appalled at the sight of a toothbrush in the bathroom? I don’t know.” With many toothbrushes now, she says, “I think there’s definitely a status symbol [aspect] to it.”

We’re more interested in oral health than ever, says Dr Zaeem Jafri, a dentist and the founder of Nova Smiles, an online advice website. “From what I’ve seen from my patients, people are more conscious about it, wanting to avoid dental treatment, wanting their teeth to look nice and feel nice, and I think a lot of people are turning to gadgets to help.” Another dentist, Dr Reena Wadia, known as Dr Reena, a periodontist or gum specialist at the RW Perio clinic in London, says: “Gum health has become super topical. One reason why is because there’s really good evidence now that gum health is linked to your general health, so gum health is now part of the wellness conversation. People are taking it more seriously.” There is growing evidence that gum disease, she says, comes with an “increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Those are the two key ones, [but] there’s lots of other conditions related to it.” A poor oral microbiome has been associated with a range of diseases, including Alzheimer’s and several types of cancer, as well as depression.

Both Dr Reena and Jafri recommend rechargeable electric toothbrushes over manual ones, but neither are urging their patients to go out and buy a Dyson brush, or spend similar sums on other brands. “There’s no robust research that says a certain kind of electric brush removes plaque at a better rate than others,” says Jafri.

Jafri has tested Dyson’s CameraJet, along with many other electric toothbrushes. He found it messy – the water jet was hard to angle, and he says it didn’t seem to find all the gaps between his teeth. He points out that a non-foaming toothpaste is needed for an adequate camera view – sold by Dyson, with the cheapest at £8.49. The live stream to a phone app was a novelty, but in reality he says it was hard to see much with water, teeth and the inside of his cheeks in the way. Cameras in toothbrushes, says Jafri, “have the potential to be good. If patients had cameras that were detecting chipped and broken fillings and can send those images to a dentist to review [and] spot things early, that would be a phenomenal advancement. For Dyson right now, it’s using the camera to detect when the brush is in the right position to shoot the water jet – it didn’t really work that well for me. It’s a bit of an overkill.”

Another concern is that the water jet rinses away the toothpaste when most dentists now recommend spitting, not rinsing, so the fluoride in it stays on and around the teeth for longer. Dr Reena adds: “[The water jet may] make people think, oh, I don’t need to floss, or I don’t need to use interdental brushes. But actually, that jet is an adjunct, not a replacement.” Niamh Turney, a Dyson engineer who worked on the CameraJet, says, however, “The goal is to make interdental cleaning easier and more convenient for those who aren’t already managing to fit flossing into their routine.”

There have been reports of some brushes overheating, and charging problems; at the time of writing, the brush was unavailable to buy. Dyson says it is aware that “a small number of early batches may have experienced a component issue. We are isolating those batches and are taking all the necessary steps to support our customers,” and that there are “some shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production. We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”

Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an oral health crisis. It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children are more than three times more likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.

The first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch and Boots, alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.

Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”

It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”

As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”

One of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”

Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”

Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.

“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”

title: Control Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomena
description:
PlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; Remedy
A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
This is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.
As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House.
fullText:
PlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; Remedy
A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe

This is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.

As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House. You’d navigate architecturally impossible spaces bridging the subconscious and the bricks-and-mortar world, in order to defeat a malevolent fridge. That’s broadly true again in Resonant, albeit with diminishing returns. This time you’re playing as Jesse’s brother Dylan, waking up after years of containment in the Oldest House to find its contents have escaped into downtown Manhattan. So you head out of the interesting place, and into a setting you’ve explored before in Marvel’s Spider-Man, The Division, Max Payne, and others ad infinitum.

It’s disappointing because being bewitchingly strange has historically been Remedy’s great strength. It’s not unusual for games to give a reverent nod to Twin Peaks now and then, but this studio is the alpha and omega of interactive Lynchian nightmares. It’s been refining that skill since 2001’s Max Payne, and at this point there’s really nobody better at nonlinear storytelling or unnerving dream sequences.

Remedy’s take on New York has an exhilaratingly free-form structure that lets you take on enemies, missions and places in roughly the order you want. The main missions are fairly rigid, but you can engage with the rest however and whenever you want. You fight a malevolent paranormal force with an imaginative collection of supernatural kung fu moves, whose power and combo potential level up satisfyingly. Your shapeshifting weapon can take many forms, from a dagger-like blade to a scythe or a hammer. Secondary attacks, ranged weapons and passive abilities lend more interest to fights against paranormal entity the Hiss as time goes on, but compared to something like the surgically precise swordplay of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, battles feel a bit blunt here.

Your ultimate tests come in the form of the Resonants themselves, a series of bosses lying in wait throughout Manhattan. Remedy’s knack for otherworldly horror comes to the fore in their visual design, which I won’t spoil, and like so much of the game they can be hunted down in any order. Beware, though – beating them changes other enemies’ presence, strength and behaviour afterwards.

Dylan’s movement is more imaginative and enjoyable than his arsenal. Here, trading off a fascinating indoor setting for more outdoor space starts to make sense, as you triple-jump your way across rooftops and shift your gravitational grounding to walk on streets that have been bent upwards vertically à la Inception. It’s playful about it, too – soon after gaining that latter ability, your bureau handler pumps some EDM down the radio to soundtrack your run through a multistorey car park whose levels fold and distort at impossible angles.

It is the little moments like this, not the grand story beats, that prove the most memorable and gratifying. Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.

title: UK not ‘on the slide’, Burnham to tell UN as he gears up for first meeting with Trump – UK politics live
description:
Burnham is heading to New York for the United Nations general assembly
According to the overnight briefing from No 10 ahead of his speech to the UN, Andy Burnham will make AI (artificial intelligence) one of the main themes of his visit to New York. Downing Street says:
Major global challenges such as AI, the conflict in Ukraine and security in the Middle East are expected to dominate the agenda of the prime minister’s meetings in New York over the next 24 hours, as world leaders converge on the city.
The prime minister is expected to use the visit to drive forward global work on AI, both to ensure it is being used as a force for good and to maximise opportunities to use the technology to deliver safety and security for people at home.
This Finnish initiative – pushing compulsory testing of Frontier AI models before release – has the backing of the leaders of Australia, Canada, Germany, the EU, Bahrain and Singapore. https://presidentti.
fullText:
Burnham is heading to New York for the United Nations general assembly

Kanishka Narayan, the minister for AI, is on the trip to New York with the PM. In a video that he recorded on the plane, he says the fact that he is going shows that AI is now “top of the international agenda”. He says his message to the industry has been “take risks seriously”.

According to the overnight briefing from No 10 ahead of his speech to the UN, Andy Burnham will make AI (artificial intelligence) one of the main themes of his visit to New York. Downing Street says:

Major global challenges such as AI, the conflict in Ukraine and security in the Middle East are expected to dominate the agenda of the prime minister’s meetings in New York over the next 24 hours, as world leaders converge on the city.

The prime minister is expected to use the visit to drive forward global work on AI, both to ensure it is being used as a force for good and to maximise opportunities to use the technology to deliver safety and security for people at home.

His speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday evening is expected to focus on AI, making the case for the international community to harness the technology for good to drive down the cost of living and support a more stable and secure world.

As part of using AI responsibly to support people at home, the prime minister will announce the launch of work between the UK and US on a new AI and Autonomy partnership. This collaboration will help the UK protect critical national infrastructure, from sea lanes to airspace – enabling us to detect threats and deter our adversaries using the latest AI technology developed on both sides of the Atlantic.

The press release implies that Burnham, at least on this trip, will be more interested in how AI can used to threaten Russia than in how steps can be taken to stop AI wiping out humanity. The press notice also says “the UK’s Ministry of Defence Rapid AI Delivery Taskforce and the US’s Department of War Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office work together on artificial intelligence and autonomy”.

Sam Coates from Sky News points out that many leading countries, as well as the European Union, yesterday backed a call from the Finnish government for compulsory safety testing of all the most advanced, frontier AI models before they are released. But the UK did not sign up, he says. He reports:

This Finnish initiative – pushing compulsory testing of Frontier AI models before release – has the backing of the leaders of Australia, Canada, Germany, the EU, Bahrain and Singapore. https://presidentti.fi/en/a-call-for-control-of-frontier-ai-models/ It’s dated yesterday 21/9. The UK will have been asked.

But Andy Burnham has not signed – and appears at the UN general assembly today to be taking a different - arguably weaker - path. Burnham is going to the UN arguing almost exactly the opposite impression: that Britain is uniquely placed to lead international AI governance, mediate between the US and China and make AI a centrepiece of its 2027 G20 presidency.

And there’s no mention of Britain backing compulsory pre-release testing of AI, unlike the other countries. The language in the press release is much more watery: he wants to ensure AI is used “for good” but avoids specifics.

Darren Jones, chief secretary to the PM when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street, has said the government should not be shunning this initiative. He says:

It’s great to see @alexstubb providing this leadership and bringing other countries together to call for pre-deployment testing.

The list of signatories to the ‘Call for Control of Frontier AI Models’ are the United Kingdom’s natural allies.

The UK has special access to American AI models through the AI Security Institute, which is partly why the UK Government will want to remain in lock step with the United States.

But I don’t see any reason why the UK can’t I encourage our government to do so and to offer to broker agreement on its application with the United States.

The comment from Andy Burnham criticising Donald Trump from 2017 quoted earlier (see 9.58am) referred to the prospect of Trump visiting Manchester during his state visit. In fact, he never went near the city. But next year he may be there, because No 10 has announced that it will host the G20 summit.

In its report on the story, the Manchester Evening News says:

The move to host the G20 in Manchester was reportedly set up months ago after Andy Burnham became prime minister, using his first phone call with Mr Trump to invite him to the city, and which is said to have been accepted by the American President.

It is understood that planning has already started for the enormous gathering, which will require the biggest security operation the city has ever seen …

Work on hosting the summit in Manchester had begun before Mr Burnham took office but the prime minister has been an enthusiastic cheerleader for the city since entering Downing Street, including establishing the No 10 North operation in the city centre.

In his huddle on the plane to the US, Andy Burnham also confirmed that the UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters. He said:

We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling.

Presumably that means Burnham won’t be agreeing with the recent report from the Campaign Against Arms Trade and the Transition Security Project saying “Britain should pay reparations to the people of Yemen for its role in crimes committed against them by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and their coalition allies during the Yemeni civil war.” It says:

Speaking to journalists on his flight to New York, Andy Burnham played down suggestions that previous critical things he has said about Donald Trump could cause a problem when they meet later.

As with almost everyone on the left of politics in the UK, Burnham has a longish record of saying disobliging things about the US president. In 2017, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said that as a “matter of principle” he would not meet Trump because of the “hateful, extremist material” he posted online. After Trump backed his supporters who stormed the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 to try to overturn the presidential election result, Burnham said: “Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now.” Only last year he accused Trump of bringing “instability to the world”.

Burnham did not apologise for any of these comments, or retract them, but he told reporters it was time to move on. He also pointed out that Trump had been dismissive of him recently, describing him as “the mayor of a town”.

Politicians say things throughout their career, but now the important thing is to focus on the moment you are in, and I did say to the president in our first phone call, I said Mr President, Manchester isn’t ‘some town’. I said ‘this is Manchester’.

And so yes, the right thing to do is to have a laugh about it, isn’t it, and move beyond it.

Asked if he could trust Trump, Burnham said:

When you come into this job, you realise how deep this relationship is. We trust our allies. Of course, we do.

Asked if he trusted Trump personally, Burnham replied: “Yes.”

(This is one of those comments best understood by applying the Mandy Rice-Davies principle, rather than taking it literally.)

Politico has a bit more colour on the huddle in today’s London Playbook.

Burnham’s first huddle with the Lobby pack on the government jet, where he sat chatting for 38 minutes in jeans, a suit jacket and his blue Joseph’s Goal wristband. It was a more discursive affair than under Starmer. The newbie PM was so disappointed that no hacks asked him to diss Danny Dyer — see here for the very sweary context— that he volunteered the line anyway. “I’m not sure I know who he is,” said Burnham. “Is he the father-in-law of a West Ham player?”

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. Pippa Crerar has the story, which is based on what Burnham told journalists as he spoke to them in what reporters call a “huddle” on his flight to New York.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is at the United Nations general assembly today and in a speech to the world (or, technically, to people in the hall and anyone watching on TV at around 2am UK time), he will say that Britain is not “on the slide”.

Speaking to reporters on the plane to New York, Burnham said:

The plan for Britain is about ‘what is our direction over the next 10 years and how do we make life more affordable for people’. That is my main priority, that’s what people are looking for.

I hear people saying the country is on the slide – we’re the fastest growing in the G7, there’s lots to be proud of, there’s a lot right with the country and I’m going to give a really upbeat message when I speak.

But the story of the day will instead focus on Burnham’s meeting with someone who does think the UK is “on the slide”, or at least claims to think that. “Your country’s in trouble. You’re on the edge of disaster,” Donald Trump told a GB News reporter recently.

In her overnight story ahead of the meeting, Pippa Crerar, who is on the trip with Burnham, says Burnham is going to adopt a middle-of-the-road approach to the US president when they meet. She says:

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as [Keir] Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

This is a reference to Starmer offering Trump an unprecedented second state visit when they first met at the White House. Theresa May also found herself pimping the monarch at her first meeting with Trump. There were good reasons for both offers at the time, and they bought both newbie PMs some goodwill from the White House monster, but it did not last and both those encounters are now recalled as moments of national embarrassment. As long as today’s meeting is cordial, Burnham will probably be happy with something more low-key.

It is hard to know what can be achieved in any meeting with Trump because he is so unpredicable. Later Burnham has another meeting with a president which will get far less coverage, but may turn out to be more consequential. The PM is meeting Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, for the first time and, with the prospects of the EU-UK reset in jeopardy, there is a lot to discuss.

Here is the agenda for the day.

9am: The final day of the Lib Dem conference in Brighton starts. The debates this morning will include one on the Lib Dems’ water policy.

2.30pm: Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, gives his keynote speech at the conference.

Around 4.45pm (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump at the UN in New York.

Late afternoon/early evening (UK time): Burnham has bilateral meetings with Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, and others.

Late evening (UK time): Burnham co-chairs a meeting on the Middle East with other leaders including Emmanuel Macron, the French president, and Mark Carney, the Canadian PM.

Around 1.50am (UK time): Burnham gives his speech to the UN before flying back to the UK.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

title: Black Tesla employees accuse company of fostering racial discrimination in major trial
description:
Lawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in California
Dozens of Black employees at Tesla’s flagship plant in California said they were subject to racist slurs, unequal pay and promotions, and bullying by supervisors on a daily basis, a situation management did little to nothing to fix.
Their complaints form the basis of a lawsuit brought against the Elon Musk-owned electric car company by the state of California, which began trial with opening statements on Monday.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Lawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in California

Dozens of Black employees at Tesla’s flagship plant in California said they were subject to racist slurs, unequal pay and promotions, and bullying by supervisors on a daily basis, a situation management did little to nothing to fix.

Their complaints form the basis of a lawsuit brought against the Elon Musk-owned electric car company by the state of California, which began trial with opening statements on Monday.

Brett Watson, a lawyer for the California Civil Rights Department, started by showing the court a series of photographs taken throughout Tesla’s Fremont factory. There was the N-word scratched on to a grey-blue metal surface and written in black marker on a wall. “KKK”, swastikas, the Confederate flag, a white supremacist logo and “go back to Africa” had also been found scrawled in bathrooms, lockers, workplace benches and lunch tables, according to court documents.

Watson listed a long string of racial epithets workers said were directed personally at them, including one incident where a Black worker said he was asked: “You want to hang from a tree?”

“Despite what Tesla might argue, you will hear Black workers were deeply offended,” Watson said. “These experiences cannot be dismissed as a few bad apples … hundreds of complaints to Tesla and [the Civil Rights Department] will show these experiences were not isolated.”

Watson said Black employees at Tesla experienced “rampant racism” that was left unchecked for years, and that workers referred to the factory as a “slaveship”, “the plantation” and “The Elon Slave Labor Association” – spelling out TESLA. One Black worker told state lawyers that he heard racial slurs as often as 50-100 times a day.

The lawsuit was filed against Tesla in February 2022 and alleges that the company did not comply with the law, violating California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act. It alleges that the factory was racially segregated and Black workers were paid less, promoted less and terminated more frequently than their white counterparts.

The state is seeking financial damages and injunctive relief, which could force Tesla to change its labor practices and internal policies. Judge Peter Borkon will make the final ruling in the bench trial, which proceeds without a jury.

It’s the first such lawsuit brought against Tesla by a government agency on behalf of dozens of workers to go to trial. Legal experts say the outcome of the trial could have sweeping consequences for the company since the state is not bound by the same arbitration agreements as employees. The trial is expected to continue through the end of October.

The car manufacturer has denied any wrongdoing and called the lawsuit “misguided”, saying it has “always disciplined and terminated employees who engage in misconduct, including those who use racial slurs or harass others in different ways”. Tesla said its Fremont factory has a majority-minority workforce and provides “the best paying jobs in the automotive industry” to tens of thousands of Californians.

Tyree Jones, the lead lawyer for Tesla, began his opening statements repeatedly saying the N-word in a familiar tone. “What’s up my [N-word], my [N-word] …,” Jones said, adding that “none of which is used as a racial slur.”

“By this action, the state of California attacks the way many Black people greet each other,” Jones said. “It’s offensive.”

Jones touted Tesla’s accomplishments as an innovative electric car manufacturer and reiterated that the company provides thousands of jobs in the state. “The most prolific employer of California is on trial and under attack by the state,” Jones said. Referring to the racist graffiti around the factory, Jones said: “The state is blaming the employer, when it’s the victim.”

After both sides presented opening arguments, the state called three witnesses. All were former Black employees at Tesla who said they either witnessed or were subject to racism at the company. The first witness worked at Tesla from 2021 to 2024 and said he was repeatedly bullied for being Black. In one incident, he alleged he was called the N-word by another employee, and the company gave him a write-up on the situation instead of the instigator.

The second witness was a senior security manager who worked at Tesla for six years. He said he habitually worked with human resources when complaints of discrimination came in, and that he witnessed Black employees treated differently than workers of other races. In one incident, he alleged Musk got involved when white employees were caught drinking alcohol on site and the CEO directed management to override company policy and not terminate the workers.

Nadia Clark, who previously worked as a police officer and an army officer for decades, was employed as a security manager at Tesla’s Fremont facility from 2020 to 2022. She testified about an incident where a white employee called her the N-word more than ten times in a row in front of other workers.

“I likened Tesla to some experiences I had on the street and in the military. It was like a pressure cooker,” Clark said. “These words have a violent landing.”

She said the incident shook her and she immediately reported it to human resources, but never got a response. Clark decided to leave Tesla that day. “There were these continuous patterns that were never addressed,” Clark said. “The work environment was unsafe, hostile, and I never returned.”

This lawsuit is one of dozens of discrimination suits brought against Tesla, including a case brought by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, a federal agency. The suits allege the company has routinely ignored complaints of repeated racial harassment. In 2022, a federal jury awarded Owen Diaz, a former Tesla employee, $137m for these claims – one of the largest awards given in a discrimination lawsuit brought by a single worker, although a judge later reduced that sum.

Similar suits have been filed by female employees, who allege they experienced physical assaults, harassment and catcalling at Tesla facilities across the country.

Tesla has denied wrongdoing in all cases, and has said it implemented various policies in recent years to prevent racist and sexist conduct and punish it when it does occur.

Musk, who joined Tesla in 2004 and became the CEO in 2008, has also been accused of racist behavior, including promoting white supremacist conspiracy theories like “white genocide”. The CEO also tends to broadcast his thoughts on X, a social media platform he owns, fixating on anti-immigrant content and theories that the white race is under threat.

Musk is not expected to be called as a witness in the trial. He hasn’t publicly addressed the legal proceedings under way and did not return a request for comment.

fullText:
Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use

British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to ​plan the massacre.

The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.

Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.

Altman published a letter ​to the community saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted ‌law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never ‌followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.

The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being ‌demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.

A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”

British Columbia’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent ‌the shooting.

Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by ​suicide.

Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.

The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.

After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the ⁠account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did ​not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law ​enforcement.

The lawsuit comes after a series of ​cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, ​including lawsuits related to a mass ‌shooting at Florida State ​University last year.

In June, Florida became the ​first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.

OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

title: Making Games with Open Code
description: Robot, build me a game
fullText:
I found myself with a tiny amount of free time while I was on parental leave earlier this year. Between taking my daughter to libraries, shovelling dirt around our garden, and returning countless toys back to their boxes, I made a little web game. You can play it at thisdungeoneternal.com.

I was attempting to use only GitHub copilot through opencode and read/edit the code myself as little as possible. This worked for scaffolding out a hello world phaser js project, starting to move a character around the screen, and getting some pixel art animations happening.

This was back in the heady days of the $10 a month GitHub copilot unlimited plan. Maybe it’s the non-frontier model I was using (Claude sonnet) but I found when given no help (only giving it instructions for features, pretending to be a non technical product manager), the agent would code itself into a bit of a mess. It seemed to get the current job done with no concern for possibilities of future changes.

It created a MainScene.js file and basically worked purely in that file until it was 1200 lines long with a whole lot of nesting. Left to its own devices it eventually got to a point where formatting and nesting issues meant that it would take a lot of time just getting curly braces in the right place and validating the js syntax. It wasn’t proactive about writing tests or using formatting/linting tools. It wouldn’t automatically refactor to DRY up code.

The nice thing about this is that we might still have jobs as developers in the future, as the agents don’t seem great at setting themselves up for success. The annoying thing is that we’re going to have to prove we’re getting a productivity boost from this stuff so we better learn to use it. Things in AI change in a rate of months, so possibly trying the same experiment today on frontier models could already produce a different result.

I think the answer I (and many others) have found is that you need as many automated (non llm) code tools to provide guard rails as possible. That means formatting, linting, testing, static analysis, anything that can take the non-deterministic output of an llm and do something deterministic with it.

After I started having more input into the code, I did manage to get some pretty cool stuff happening with opencode and sonnet. I got it to program the music so a randomized low pass filter and wet/dry reverb balance would apply to the background music. This was all written with web APIs which would have taken me days (maybe weeks) of research to work out. It’s also so nice to not have to watch a YouTube video or read a bunch of docs to do something basic in a library you’re unfamiliar with. You just explain in plain English and you at least get something you can edit.

Another thing is that I spent BARELY any time on the game. I had so little spare time in the period I was making the game. This game would not exist without opencode. I might have the scaffold of it completed, but none of the nice menus, animations, or mobile support.

All the sound effects, music, and in-game sprites were NOT made with AI. I had a go at creating pixel art assets and it didn’t work for me at all. There are some paid tools out there that are specifically for generating AI pixel art. I didn't try these, but I’m sure those would get you further than chatbots. Instead, I bought the sprites I bought from itch.io. I did a lot of the voice acting personally. I used a tool called ardour and some free VSTs to make the music. Some of the sounds were from Wikimedia open commons. I only used llms for the code and for the hero image of the castle.

I think if tried to create the assets of the game with AI tools it would have felt a lot worse. I’m sure all the voice acting, recording, music and art could be higher quality and some parts of what an llm would generate sound/look be more professional. But I think for these assets, I’d rather see/hear amateur work than AI generated work. For creative pursuits, our fleshy monkey brains remain necessary.

title: C3 0.8.4: The Last Keyword Renaming Before the Syntax Freeze
description: C3 is the ergonomic, safe evolution of C. Familiar syntax, full ABI compatibility, optionals, slices, contracts and zero-cost abstractions.
fullText:
C3 0.8.4 is now available. This release expands parameter reflection and contracts, adds configurable stack probing and stack protection, introduces iOS support, and brings a new collection type and stream utilities to the standard library.

This release is titled “The Last Renaming” because it very likely contains the final adjustments to C3’s keyword set – and I think we’ve finally got them right.

Changing keywords is hardly the best way to convey stability, but sometimes it is necessary. In C3's case 0.9.0 means syntactic freeze of the language, so getting the choice right in the 0.8.x cycle is vital.

Of course, as usual the old keywords will still work as part of the backwards compatibility with 0.8.3 and earlier, but moving to the new ones are recommended.

faultdef and attrdef were introduced in 0.7.0 and constdef in 0.7.10. The idea was to unify them under an easy-to-remember "def" suffix. Unfortunately a downside is that this pushes them to retain a similar syntactic shape. After much discussion, we're experimentally introducing new names:

excuse comes from the general terminology, where the fault returned for an empty optional is called the "excuse" in the documentation. That this becomes a keyword further cements that term. In addition, excuse gains a shape with {}, not supported by faultdef:

attrmacro was chosen because attrdef takes parameters and in general acts closer to a macro than an alias.

Both cenum and constset were considered. Eventually the latter won out because it establishes a stronger independent feature, whereas the cenum hints at it just being an "enum that works like in C", which isn't correct.

Note that attrdef, constdef and faultdef will work throughout the entire 0.8.x cycle. The new keywords are considered an experimental change, and will be evaluated until 0.9.0. It will become the standard in 0.9.0 only if it's decided that the names are an improvement.

It is now possible to associate a requirement with a particular parameter by placing it in brackets after @require:

This lets diagnostics point directly to the argument responsible for a failed precondition, making contract failures easier to understand at the call site.

Parameter reflection is more capable in 0.8.4. $reflect(foo).param_struct and Foo::param_struct provide access to a function's parameters as a struct. This allows macros to build up calls by populating each field, and then use struct splat to make the call:

Parameters can now also carry @tag attributes, and reflected parameters support get_tag, tags, and has_tag.

It is also possible to inspect a parameter's default value through .default_value.

As part of this work, FooFn::params now returns reflected references rather than ReflectedParam values. Code using this reflection API may need to be updated.

Alias definitions now accept ternary expressions. This makes it possible to select an implementation using a feature flag without wrapping the alias in a separate conditional declaration:

C3 0.8.4 adds several controls for stack hardening. The new --stack-probe, --stack-probe-size, and --stack-protector options configure stack probing and stack-canary generation from the command line.

Individual functions and lambdas can override these settings with @stackprobe(level), @nostackprobe, @stackprotector(level), and @nostackprotector. Naked functions no longer receive stack protectors by default.

The new @noredzone attribute disables use of the x86-64 red zone for a function. As a temporary safety measure, functions on ELF x86-64 are emitted without red-zone use. ELF and COFF output also gained support for the dso_local attribute.

The --implicit-float setting provides control over the emission of floating-point operations. This is useful for low-level targets where implicitly generated floating-point instructions are undesirable.

This release adds support for targeting iOS. LLVM compilation scheduling has also been adjusted so the largest modules are built first, helping make better use of parallel compilation.

Project target types benchmark and test now work correctly with c3c benchmark and c3c test, including targeted benchmark functions. Project names passed to c3c init may now contain -, and the new --keep-obj option preserves object files after building and linking.

The compiler can now warn about unused locals and parameters with --warn-unusedlocal and --warn-unusedparam. Diagnostics have been improved for incorrect panic-function names, excessively long source lines or underlines, and build options incorrectly written with =.

Equality comparisons between slices of flat types are now lowered to memcmp instead of scalar loops, reducing the cost of comparing suitable slices.

The standard library now includes CachedInStream and CachedOutStream, as well as the new std::collections::Tree collection.

InStream.read has been made consistent: it returns 0 at end of file instead of throwing io::EOF, and it now requires a non-empty destination buffer. Code which catches io::EOF from InStream.read should be updated to check the returned byte count instead.

Ranges gained a range::slice macro, and Path.is_link can be used to determine whether a path is a symbolic link.

Sockets can now report both ends of a connection through Socket.peer_address, Socket.peer_port, Socket.local_address, and Socket.local_port. Logging gained log::get_logger.

RefCounted has been reworked slightly to differentiate between finalization and freeing.

The old deprecated pool::ThreadPool is now disabled by default, and the new thread::ThreadPool is enabled by default. The old implementation is exposed as ThreadPoolOld, with -D OLD_THREADPOOL available for restoring the old name, for projects that do not want to change the name to ThreadPoolOld.

This release fixes a broad set of compiler crashes and miscompilations, particularly around generics, vectors, bitstruct operations, default arguments, and deferred control flow.

Notable compiler fixes include:

The standard library also received several correctness fixes. Large left shifts now work for BigInt, copying a DString no longer overwrites its allocator, and FixedBlockPool handles changes to grow_capacity correctly. Fixes also landed for mem::equals, UTF-16 surrogate pairs in String.escape, virtual-memory reserve page sizes, and stale thread IDs returned by thread::current on POSIX.

String case-conversion attributes such as @str_pascalcase and @str_camelcase now retain digits instead of treating them as discarded word separators.

Again, this release wouldn't have been possible without the C3 community. I'd like to extend a deep thank you to everyone who contributed through code, issue reports, testing, and discussions.

Stdlib: Archishman Nag, m0tholith, Manu Linares, Ricardo Tomasi, Senthilnathan, Velikiy Kirill.

Compiler & toolchain: Alexandru Paniș, Darvisim, Manu Linares, neerajnangireddy, rickyadastra, ssimb, Vyacheslav Denisov.

CI/Infrastructure: Darvisim, Fernando López Guevara, Manu Linares.

Check out the documentation or download it and try it out.

title: Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?
description: OpenAI’s proof seems eligible for a $1-million prize—but only by using a controversial loophole
fullText:
Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?

OpenAI’s proof seems eligible for a $1-million prize—but only by using a controversial loophole

Read about how mathematicians are dealing with the AI takeover of their field in our feature here.

Two weeks ago OpenAI claimed a solution to one of the biggest open problems in math—the Navier-Stokes problem—an achievement worth a $1-million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute. The proof ignited a powder keg of concern over artificial intelligence companies’ race to disrupt the subject.

But with the dust still far from settled, a different controversy is emerging: Did OpenAI even solve the right Navier-Stokes problem?

Generated by an internal large language model (LLM), OpenAI’s proof relies on an approach that many experts find unnatural. It solves a variant of the problem that mathematicians say is disconnected from reality and thus less interesting. In a sense, the LLM found and exploited a loophole in the framing of the question.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“The most important problem is unsolved,” says Luis Silvestre, a mathematician at the University of Chicago. “The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.”

Furthermore, last Thursday, three mathematicians posted a proof of their own that showed that OpenAI’s method can never be extended to solve the full problem. In other words, the loophole will never be closed, barring some completely new idea.

The Navier-Stokes equations are supposed to describe how fluids flow, but mathematicians doubt whether they can always be trusted. The million-dollar problem is about whether the equations ever “blow up,” which would mean they’d allow the flow to be infinitely fast at points—something that can’t happen in the real world.

But there’s one piece of the equations that’s optional—sometimes it’s there; sometimes it isn’t. The “it” here is an external force such as gravity that affects how a fluid moves. “All fluids we know of are under some kind of external force,” says mathematician Diego Córdoba. “So to have the force makes complete sense.”

When most experts think about the Navier-Stokes problem, though, it’s without this force. They want to find a purer, more fundamental way for the equations to blow up by using only the intrinsic forces within any fluid—not by applying some specific, precisely contrived external force. “Most of the other groups, it’s true, were specifically considering the scenario without a force,” says mathematician Luis Martínez-Zoroa.

In the past few years, though, Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa put all their focus on this niche piece of the equations and laid out a method to build a very specific external force to trigger a blowup. On September 7 two other mathematicians used their program (and AI) to produce a blowup for a frictionless fluid—considered a major step toward blowing up Navier-Stokes. OpenAI finished the job less than a day later—timing that has led to a heated dispute between the latter two mathematicians and the company.

But the new work released last Thursday shows unequivocally that if the force is removed, the blowup will disappear. OpenAI’s method can never work, in fact, without using a very contrived equation for the force that is unlike anything that could occur in the real world. “They essentially prove that the formulation with an external force was different from the problem we really wanted to solve,” Silvestre says.

In other words, the LLM’s result does not—and will never—answer the Navier-Stokes problem that mathematicians really care about.

It did, however, unambiguously solve the problem according to the Clay Institute’s original formulation. The official problem statement, penned in 2000 by mathematician Charles Fefferman, offers an option called “C,” in which solutions are allowed to use an external force like OpenAI’s.

Now fluid dynamicists are grappling with a possibility few had considered before: the idea that the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up but only with an external force. In this scenario, you can mathematically place a fluid in a specific, unrealistic situation to break the equations, yet the blowup can never come from the fluid itself.

“It’s really uncertain at this moment,” says mathematician Gonzalo Cao-Labora. “Depending on the answer to this, I think the contribution of OpenAI will be regarded differently.” If it turns out to be true, he adds, “people would probably think about the Clay problem and say, ‘We shouldn’t have put the external force in the statement.’”

This might even be good news for “team humanity.” LLMs are great at finding blowups that exist—at searching the infinite landscape of fluid scenarios and plucking out the precise situation that breaks the equations. But proving that blow-up is impossible is a kind of math AI still struggles with. “We may be at less of a disadvantage, or maybe an advantage, compared to LLMs,” says Cao-Labora. “LLMs are especially good at constructing things that are very explicit and not as good—for now—in making new theory.”

But regardless of whether the path to solving the full Navier-Stokes problem requires a clever new blowup or a whole new mathematical discipline, everyone is becoming more hesitant to bet against the machines.

“We are really amazed with how [the technology] has evolved in the last year—so we don't know how it will look in one year,” says Cao-Labora. “It’s really a wake-up call to the community.”

title: Tesla's record month: 4 fatal Autopilot and Full Self-Driving crashes
description: July 2026 set a record for Tesla driver-assist crashes: 236, including 4 fatal ones the public never connected to Autopilot or FSD.
fullText:
July 2026 was the worst month on record for Tesla driver-assist crashes. Tesla reported 236 of them to federal regulators, the most it has ever filed in a single month.

Four of those crashes killed someone. In every one, Tesla’s own data says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, and in every one, the public was never told the system was involved. This is the latest from our ongoing investigation matching Tesla’s redacted NHTSA reports to real, named crashes.

Under a 2021 NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact. Tesla’s monthly count has climbed all year, from 135 in March to 207 in May to 209 in June. July’s 236 is a new high.

Each of these appears in Tesla’s July filings, each marked “Verified Engaged” — meaning Tesla confirmed through its telematics that the system was on. And on each one, Tesla redacted the three fields that would explain the crash: the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area.

At Electrek, we matched the non-redacted facts about each crash to public reports to better understand each one, since Tesla is trying to limit the information.

Upper Marlboro, Maryland. Around 12:45 a.m. on July 12, a Tesla Model 3 making a left turn onto Governor’s Park Lane off Route 301 failed to yield to a Harley-Davidson going straight, Maryland State Police said. Three people died: the motorcyclist, Matthew Vowell, 48; his passenger, Krystal Vowell, 47; and a passenger inside the Tesla, Adriana Maxwell, 22. The Tesla was operating as a rideshare. Tesla’s report logs a left turn at 20 mph, driver-assist verified engaged, and says it holds the video. An unprotected left turn across oncoming traffic is a City-Streets maneuver, the kind of thing FSD does and basic Autopilot cannot, the same failure mode as the Batavia crash we documented.

San Mateo, California. On July 15, a 2016 Tesla Model S left the road, struck a light pole, and caught fire, killing its driver. Tesla’s report: driver-assist verified engaged, 52 mph, a solo strike of a fixed object. It’s a road departure, the single most common crash type in Tesla’s entire driver-assist file.

Ione, California. Around 7:18 a.m. on July 22, a Tesla heading north on Highway 104 crossed into the southbound lane, sideswiped a Honda, and hit a Cadillac head-on, according to the California Highway Patrol. The Tesla’s driver, Shelby Waldie, 25, was killed; a 2-year-old in the car was hospitalized. Investigators said the reason it crossed the center line is under investigation. Tesla’s report: a brand-new 2026 Model Y, verified engaged, 54 mph. The reason it crossed is the redacted narrative.

Ashby, Minnesota. Around 3:57 p.m. on July 20, on Interstate 94 in a work zone, a westbound Ford collided with an eastbound Tesla, and a third vehicle then struck them, the Minnesota State Patrol said. Two people died: the Tesla’s driver, Harold Ennulat, 73, and the Ford’s driver, 24. Here, the police made it sound like the Ford was going the wrong way, so the engaged Tesla was likely not to blame. But Tesla’s data still shows the system on at 50 mph, and Tesla holds the EDR and the video.

None of the four was reported publicly as involving Autopilot or FSD. In each, the only reason anyone can connect the death to a driver-assist system is that Tesla had to file a report, which it then redacted.

There’s a second problem buried in these filings. Tesla’s report lists a single “highest injury severity.” In Upper Marlboro, three people died, and in Ashby, two did, yet each report records one fatality. Tesla’s federal filings undercount the dead in its driver-assist crashes, which means every aggregate built from this data, including safety comparisons Tesla itself points to, starts low.

Almost no other automaker does this. GM runs a comparable connected-fleet system in Super Cruise and redacts none of its crash narratives. Across the current file, Tesla hides the narrative on 100% of its reports; GM, 0%.

This is the heart of the investigation. Tesla is, more than ever, pushing owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it drives itself, selling the software as “Full Self-Driving” while the human stays legally responsible at all times. Then it seals the records that would show how the system behaves when things go wrong, telling regulators it would “suffer financial harm” if the public saw them. A motorcyclist, a rideshare passenger, a 25-year-old with her toddler in the car, a 73-year-old man: four people dead in one month, in cars Tesla’s own data says were driving themselves, and not one of those reports says what the car did.

I'd love to see the data on here with the crash involving a Model S that took place near Madison (WI) about 2 years ago. Car somehow went off the road and hit a tree. If I recall, there were 5 people inside and all 5 perished after the doors could not be opened and the car burned. One of the 5 inside was a friend of my nephew's.

We’ve now matched more than a dozen of these, one by one, from Clute to Moraine, and July made the point in a single month: as the crash count climbs to record highs, the fatal cases keep surfacing in Tesla’s data and staying out of the public record. Some of these deaths, like the Minnesota one, may not be Tesla’s fault at all. That’s exactly why the narratives should be open, because right now no one outside Tesla can tell the difference between a crash the system caused and one it didn’t.

We’re careful about the claim. A system being engaged within 30 seconds of a crash doesn’t prove it caused the crash, and the redacted software field means we can’t even separate Autopilot from FSD. But that uncertainty is Tesla’s doing. It has the data, it filed the reports, and it decided that what its cars did in four fatal crashes is a trade secret. Tesla is already under NHTSA investigation over how it reports these crashes. Until the narratives open up, we’ll keep matching them.

Even in the Minnesota crash, which I conceded might not sound like Tesla is at fault, the data and crash narrative might still be useful. Maybe the driver was on FSD, not paying attention, and could have avoided or mitigated the crash if they were.
