title: How to Make Your Code Reviewer Fall in Love with You
description: Best practices for code review when you’re the author.
fullText:
When people talk about code reviews, they focus on the reviewer. But the developer who writes the code is just as important to the review as the person who reads it. There’s scarcely any guidance on preparing your code for review, so authors often screw up this process out of sheer ignorance.

This article describes best practices for participating in a code review when you’re the author. In fact, by the end of this post, you’re going to be so good at sending out your code for review that your reviewer will literally fall in love with you.

They’re going to fall in love with you. Deal with it. Nobody ever complained on their deathbed that too many people fell in love with them.

Improving code review technique helps your reviewer, your team, and, most importantly: you.

Learn faster: If you prepare your changelist properly, it directs your reviewer’s attention to areas that support your growth rather than boring style violations. When you demonstrate an appreciation for constructive criticism, your reviewer provides better feedback .

Make others better: Your code review techniques set an example for your colleagues. Effective author practices rub off on your teammates, which makes your job easier when they send code to you.

Minimize team conflicts: Code reviews are a common source of friction. Approaching them deliberately and conscientiously minimizes arguments.

This advice sounds obvious, but I often see authors treat their reviewers like personal quality assurance technicians. These authors make zero effort to catch their own errors or to design their changelist for reviewability.

Your teammate arrives at work each day with a finite supply of focus. If they allocate some of it to you, that’s time they can’t spend on their own work. It’s only fair that you maximize the value of their time.

Reviews drastically improve when both participants trust each other. Your reviewer puts in more effort when they can count on you to take their feedback seriously. Viewing your reviewer as an obstacle you have to overcome limits the value they offer you.

Before sending code to your teammate, read it yourself. Don’t just check for mistakes — imagine reading the code for the first time. What might confuse you?

I find it helpful to take a break between writing my code and reviewing it. People often fire off their changes at the end of the day, but that’s when you’re most likely to overlook careless errors. Wait until morning, and look at the changelist with fresh eyes before handing it over to your teammate.

Adopt your reviewer’s environment as much as possible. Use the same diff view that they’ll see. It’s easier to catch dumb mistakes in a diff view than in your regular source editor.

Don’t expect yourself to be perfect. Inevitably, you’ll send out a changelist with debugging code that you forgot to delete or a stray file you meant to exclude. These mistakes aren’t the end of the world, but they’re worth tracking. Pay attention to your patterns of error, and think about creating systems to prevent them. If they happen too frequently, it signals to your reviewer that you don’t value their time.

At my last job, I met regularly with a senior engineer as part of a developer mentorship program. Before our first meeting, he asked me to bring a design document I’d written. As I handed it to him, I explained what the project was and how it aligned with my team’s goals. My mentor frowned. “Everything you just told me should be on the first page of your design doc,” he said, bluntly.

He was right. I wrote the design document imagining how my teammates would read it, but I failed to consider other readers. There was a broader audience beyond my immediate teammates that included partner teams, mentors, and promotion committees. They should all be able to understand the document as well. Since that discussion, I always think about how to frame my work to explain its context.

Your changelist description should summarize any background knowledge the reader needs. You might have a code reviewer in mind when you write the description, but they don’t necessarily have the context you imagine. Besides, your other teammates might need to read this changelist as well, and readers in the future should understand your intentions when they look back on the change history.

A good changelist description explains what the change achieves, at a high level, and why you’re making this change.

For a deeper dive into excellent changelist descriptions, see my article, “How to Write Useful Commit Messages.”

If you rely on your reviewer to tell you when your curly braces are on the wrong line or that your change broke the automated test suite, you’re wasting their time.

Automated tests should be part of your team’s standard workflow. The review begins after all automated checks pass in a continuous integration environment.

If your team is woefully misguided and refuses to invest in continuous integration, automate these checks yourself. Add git pre-commit hooks, linters, and formatters to your development environment to ensure that your code observes proper conventions and preserves intended behavior on each commit.

What’s wrong with this picture?

The author helped me understand the function, but what about the next person who reads it? Should they dive into the change history and read every code review discussion ever? Worse is when the author comes over to my desk to give me an in-person explanation, which both interrupts my focus and ensures that nobody else ever has access to the information.

When your reviewer expresses confusion about how the code works, the solution isn’t to explain it to that one person. You need to explain it to everyone.

The best way to answer someone’s question is to refactor the code and eliminate the confusion. Can you rename things or restructure logic to make it more clear? Code comments are an acceptable solution, but they’re strictly inferior to code that documents itself naturally.

Scope creep is a common anti-pattern in code reviews. A developer starts to fix a logic bug, but they notice a UI blemish in the process. “While I’m here,” they think, “I’ll just fix this other thing.” But now they’ve muddled things. Their reviewer has to figure out which changes serve goal A and which serve goal B.

The best changelists just Do One Thing. The smaller and simpler the change, the easier it is for the reviewer to keep all the context in their head. Decoupling unrelated changes also allows you to parallelize your reviews across teammates, reducing turnaround time for your changes.

The corollary to minimizing scope is separating functional and non-functional changes.

Developers inexperienced with code reviews often violate this rule. They’ll make a two-line change, and then their code editor automatically reformats the entire file. The developer either fails to recognize what they did or decides that the new formatting is better. They send out a two-line functional change buried in hundreds of lines of non-functional whitespace changes.

Jumbled changelists are a massive insult to your reviewer. Whitespace-only changes are easy to review. Two-line changes are easy to review. Two-line functional changes lost in a sea of whitespace changes are tedious and maddening.

Developers also tend to mix changes inappropriately while refactoring. I love it when my teammates refactor code, but I hate it when they refactor while changing the code’s behavior.

If a piece of code requires refactoring and behavioral changes, it should happen in two to three changelists:

Overly large changelists are the ugly cousins of scope creep. Suppose a developer finds that in order to introduce feature X, they must modify semantics of existing libraries A and B. If it’s a small set of changes, that’s fine, but too many of these sprawling modifications can make the changelist enormous.

A changelist’s complexity grows exponentially with the number of code lines it touches. When my changes exceed 400 lines of production code, I look for opportunities to break it up before requesting a review.

Instead of changing everything at once, can you change the dependencies first and add the new feature in a subsequent changelist? Can you keep the codebase in a sane state if you add half of the feature now and the other half in the next changelist?

It’s tedious to break up your code to find a subset that makes a working, intelligible change, but it yields better feedback and puts less strain on your reviewer.

The fastest way to ruin a code review is to take feedback personally. This is challenging, as many developers take pride in their work and see it as an extension of themselves. If your reviewer tactlessly frames their feedback as a personal attack, it’s even harder.

As the author, you ultimately control your reaction to feedback. Treat your reviewer’s notes as an objective discussion about the code, not your personal worth as a human. Responding defensively will only make things worse.

I try to interpret all notes as helpful lessons. When a reviewer catches an embarrassing bug in my code, my first instinct is to make excuses. Instead, I catch myself and praise my reviewer for their scrupulousness.

Surprisingly, it’s a good sign when your reviewer spots subtle flaws in your code. It indicates that you’re packaging your changelists well. Without all the obvious issues like bad formatting and confusing names, your reviewer can focus deeply on logic and design, yielding more valuable feedback.

From time to time, reviewers are flat out wrong. Just as you can accidentally write buggy code, your reviewer can misunderstand correct code.

Many developers react to reviewer mistakes with defensiveness. They take it as an affront that someone would insult their code with criticisms that aren’t even true.

Even when your reviewer is mistaken, that’s still a red flag. If they misread it, will others make the same mistake? Does the reader have to exercise an abnormal level of scrutiny to reassure themselves that a particular bug isn’t there?

Look for ways to refactor the code, or add comments that make the code more obviously correct. If the confusion stems from obscure language features, rewrite your code using mechanisms that are intelligible to non-experts.

I frequently run into a scenario where I give someone notes, they update their code to address some of my feedback, but they don’t write any replies. Now, we’re in an ambiguous state. Did they miss my other notes, or are they still working? If I begin a new round of review, I’m potentially wasting my time on a half-finished changelist. If I wait, I might create a deadlock where both of us are expecting the other to continue.

Establish conventions on your team that make it clear who’s “holding the baton” at any point. Either the author is working on edits, or the reviewer is writing feedback. There should never be a situation where the process stalls because nobody knows who’s doing what. You can accomplish this easily with changelist-level comments that indicate when you’re handing control back and forth.

For every note that requires action, respond explicitly to confirm that you’ve addressed it. Some code review tools allow you to mark comments as resolved. Otherwise, follow a simple convention, like, “Done,” for each note. If you disagree with the note, politely explain why you declined to take action.

Adjust your response based on your reviewer’s effort. If they write a detailed note to help you learn something new, don’t just mark it done. Respond thoughtfully to show gratitude for their effort.

Sometimes code review notes leave too much room for interpretation. When you receive a comment like, “This function is confusing,” you probably wonder what “confusing” means, exactly. Is the function too long? Is the name unclear? Does it require more documentation?

For a long time, I struggled to clarify ambiguous notes without sounding defensive. My instinct was to ask, “What’s confusing about it?” but that comes across as grouchy.

Once, I unintentionally sent a vague note to my teammate, and he responded in a way that I found fantastically disarming:

I love this response because it signals a lack of defensiveness and openness to criticism. Whenever a reviewer gives me unclear feedback, I always respond with some variation of, “What would be helpful?”

Another useful technique is to guess your reviewer’s intent and proactively edit your code based on that assumption. For a note like, “this is confusing,” give your code a second look. Usually, there’s something you can do to improve clarity. A revision communicates to your reviewer that you’re amenable to change, even if it’s not the one they had in mind.

In tennis, when you’re unsure if your opponent’s serve landed out of bounds, you give them the benefit of the doubt. There should be a similar expectation for code reviews.

Some decisions about code are a matter of personal taste. If your reviewer thinks your 8-line function would be better as two 5-line functions, neither of you is objectively “right.” It’s a matter of opinion which version is better.

When your reviewer makes a suggestion, and you each have roughly equal evidence to support your position, defer to your reviewer. Between the two of you, they have a better perspective on what it’s like to read this code fresh.

A few months ago, a user contributed a small change to an open-source project I maintain. I gave them feedback within hours, but they promptly disappeared. I checked again a few days later, and there was still no response.

Six weeks later, the mysterious developer reappeared to submit their revisions. While I appreciated their effort, the lag between rounds of review had doubled my workload. Not only did I have to re-read their code, but I also had to re-read my feedback to restore my memory of the discussion. Had they followed up within a day or two, I wouldn’t have had to do all that extra work.

A six-week pause is extreme, but I frequently see long, unnecessary delays among teammates. Someone sends out a changelist for review, receives feedback, then puts it on the back burner for a week because another task distracted them.

In addition to the time lost in restoring context, half-finished changelists increase complexity. They make it harder for everyone to keep track of what’s already merged and what’s in-flight. With more partially-complete changelists, there are more merge conflicts, and nobody likes fixing those.

Once you send your code out, driving the review to completion should be your highest priority. Delays on your end waste time for your reviewer and increase complexity for your whole team.

As you prepare your next changelist for review, consider the factors you control, and use them to guide the review productively. As you participate in reviews, look for patterns that stall progress or waste effort.

Remember the golden rule: value your reviewer’s time. A reviewer generates high-quality feedback when you allow them to focus on the interesting parts of your code. If you require them to untangle your code or police simple mistakes, you both suffer.

Lastly, communicate thoughtfully. It’s frighteningly easy for simple miscommunications or thoughtless comments to derail a review. Emotions run hot when critiquing someone else’s work, so be conscious of pitfalls that could make your reviewer feel attacked or disrespected.

Congratulations! If you’ve reached this point, you’re now an expert reviewee. Your reviewer is likely in love with you, so treat them well.

Illustrations by Loraine Yow. Edited by Samantha Mason.

title: Wikipedia's Plan to Survive the Answer Engine Apocalypse
description: At Brandweek, the nonprofit’s director of brand explained why ubiquity without attribution is an existential threat, and how a new campaign aims to fix it.
fullText:
This story was originally published in On Background with Mark Stenberg, a free, weekly newsletter that explores the key themes shaping the media industry. You can 

Wikipedia has spent 25 years building a reputation as one of the most trusted sources on the web.

Now, as answer engines rewrite how people find information online, that reputation faces a threat familiar to many publishers: ubiquity without credit.

According to the search engine measurement Ahrefs, ChatGPT cites Wikipedia more than almost any other single source, second only to Reddit. And yet, fewer humans are visiting the site itself to read, and more importantly, to edit.

As a nonprofit with a minimal reliance on advertising, Wikipedia is somewhat insulated from the traffic erosion crushing other publishers. That makes it a revealing case study in how institutions are rethinking relevance in the AI era.

At Brandweek, I asked Zack McCune, the global head of brand marketing at the Wikimedia Foundation, how the organization is responding.

Mark: Wikipedia just launched a brand campaign, created by the agency Kin, to celebrate its 25th anniversary. What prompted the campaign?

Zack: Wikipedia is 25 years old, which is quite a milestone. But we hit 25 at the exact time our relationship to knowledge is changing, and Wikipedia is at risk of becoming invisible—invisible to us and invisible to our awareness. When you search for something today, your voice assistant is giving you the answer, or your AI agent is giving you the answer, hiding the fact that, more often than not, the answer is coming from Wikipedia. For an organization that relies on hundreds of thousands of volunteers and hundreds of millions of donors, it was crucial to generate a whole new wave of support and create not only awareness but connection and engagement.

Mark: Why did you feel this was necessary, and what sort of goals were you hoping to accomplish?

Zack: Wikipedia is the backbone of knowledge on the internet, the backbone of its most trusted elements. And yet what we’re noticing on a brand health level is decline: decline in stability, a decline even in awareness or likability. It’s strange, because a lot of brands are thinking, “How do I get my content into the AI platforms?” I don’t have that problem. My content is everywhere, and yet the brand problem remains. We’re more visible than ever, and yet less known. Part of why we came to Kin, wanting to make our 25th birthday a big, splashy, emotionally driven project, was trying to get people to feel something for the knowledge they rely on. We do brand work globally all the time, but this was actually one of the first, one of the biggest campaigns done domestically in the U.S.

Mark: That was a bit of a canary in the coal mine, because brand awareness in the U.S. is usually not a problem for an institution like Wikipedia.

Zack: I’ve been with the Foundation leading brand for almost 11 years, and in that time I mostly worked on projects in Nigeria, India, Iraq, South Africa—places where we wanted to grow awareness. For us, brand awareness isn’t a metric by itself. Brand awareness becomes usage, and usage becomes editing. So the more people who know our platform and use it, the more complete our knowledge record is. It’s a public library where sooner or later we say, “We’d like you to write a book—could you do that on something you love?” We’ve been doing regional marketing for a decade. But as we moved into an underperforming market here, that’s exactly where we said: We need to do something bigger in the U.S. and Europe.

Mark: This is something I cover a lot at Adweek: websites disappearing as search engines change. Normally the concern for publishers is commercial: People aren’t coming to the website, they’re losing ad revenue. Wikipedia doesn’t have that same acute commercial exposure. But you were describing the real conversion problem as visitors to contributors, which I hadn’t thought about before. Is that the real “disappearing” issue for you, losing the people who contribute to the site?

Zack: That’s right. Year over year we see about an 8% decline in human traffic. We separate that from bot traffic, which is way up, crushing our servers. But when fewer humans make it to the site, that’s where the knowledge itself is composed. If you see a typo, if you realize something’s missing or wrong in an article, that’s where it gets fixed. All the composition happens on our site. So we’re thrilled about the distribution of knowledge through AI platforms, but we also need to constantly refresh and fact-check that content, and that means people have to come back to the homepage.

Mark: I’d love to return to the core thesis here. The aim of this campaign was to raise awareness of Wikipedia because it’s not as visible in search engines anymore, and that’s increasingly where people get their information. That’s a problem publishers across the internet are facing. One solution a lot of sites are taking is what one CEO called the “woo and sue” approach: You either strike a content licensing deal or you take AI companies to court. I know Wikipedia has some licensing arrangements. Can you talk about how Wikipedia is responding to AI as an organization, and how it plans to show up on the internet going forward?

Zack: We have an amazing group of people working on an enterprise offering, a real-time API for LLM companies that need tons of data very quickly, delivered in the way they’re used to programming against. That’s designed to do two things: get our content out on these platforms, and create a commercial relationship where the platforms themselves pay us for that usage. It’s a way to expand beyond the 8 million donors giving an average of $11 to sustain the Foundation, because we want to make sure these companies are paying their fair share too. We’re working with every major AI/LLM company you can think of, trying to establish a virtuous relationship. I hear the word “sustainable” a lot, but that feels too low-stakes. We have to anticipate 2028, 2029, and beyond. How do we keep a human content community in a position to keep all of this fact-checked for these platforms? That’s what we’re building right now. We’ve got deals underway, some public, and I hope more to come.

Mark: Your mission is to keep the world’s information accurate and free, and however people find that, it’s a win for you. So the north star is a little different from a standard website. Is that fair to say?

Zack: It is. I think the advantage we have, which is unique, is that we’re a nonprofit. We’re sustaining a mission: knowledge for the world across 300 languages and counting. What we used to worry about was losing volunteers, the community of fact-checkers and writers. It’s not about converting you to a paid subscriber, and we have no ads. The knowledge itself should go everywhere. But we need the cycle to be virtuous, so people come back and edit.

Mark: I want to talk a bit about how you think about balancing Wikipedia’s dual identity. It’s an institution, a brand, and yet it also gets the benefit of being seen as made up of thousands of individual contributors, so you get both institutional trust and creator-style trust. Do you think of Wikipedia as a brand, or as an assembly of creators?

Zack: That’s a hard question to answer. Wikipedia often gets referred to as “according to Wikipedia,” which makes it sound like “according to the New York Times,” like a single publisher’s voice, and that’s not accurate. It’s really “according to the 480 people who edited this article and reached this consensus view in the past 24 hours.” So we’re actually trying to emphasize the people more—get them from behind the page to the front of the page. The 25th anniversary campaign is entirely composed of screenshots from like 700 Wikipedia pages. That’s the platform—we’re trying to break it back into its atomic units. These are the edits. These are the statements. These are the images. And these are the people who make it happen.

Politico Decoded (EXCLUSIVE): After 15 years of Politico Pro, the global politics publisher is finally launching a second subscription product. Called Decoded (not to be confused with The Verge’s Decoder), the product bills itself as “Playbook meets Dealbook” for the technology policy sector, according to Politico CEO Goli Sheikholeslami. Whereas Pro, an enterprise subscription, costs north of five figures, Decoded will stay below $1,000 annually. The demand is certainly there—the same strategists advising politicians in D.C. are now counseling AI executives in Silicon Valley—but it will be interesting to see whether Decoded acts as a conversion funnel to Pro or attracts and retains an entirely separate audience.

Heatmap Heat (EXCLUSIVE): The climate news publisher Heatmap, launched three years ago, has stayed largely beneath the radar despite setting an admirable precedent for sustainable growth among media startups. The 20-person organization is on track to bring in $5 million in revenue this year, profitably, thanks in part to the growth of its Heatmap Pro enterprise product, whose 40 or so clients are now responsible for roughly 50% of its overall revenue. In particular, the publisher has seen outsized demand for its coverage of data centers, and it has used original polling and permitting tracking to cover the patchwork of nationwide regulation governing the controversial industry.

Realtor Repast: Next month, I’ll be hosting a private lunch during Advertising Week for telecommunications leaders on Oct. 7. The event will be hosted in partnership with Realtor.com, and the conversation will center around the unique opportunity that phases of disruption—moving, specifically—present to brands. I have partnered with the folks at Realtor a few times now, and in each instance have found the subject matter—the housing market, generational wealth, the psychological heft of relocation—immensely fascinating. If you’re interested in joining me, please reach out to liz@adweek.com.

Howl Hurting (EXCLUSIVE): Last week, I scooped that the affiliate platform Howl had sold its creator business to the Taboola-owned firm Connexity. After looking further into the matter, it appears Howl had once again fallen behind on its payments, both to creators and publishers, just as it had when I unearthed these issues originally. Connexity has since paid off any outstanding debts to the creators whose business it acquired, part of a broader effort to win over their relationships with brands, but several publishers remain unpaid, according to two sources. Howl, for its part, has no plans to let these issues stop it. According to founder Li Haslett Chen, it now has its sights set on the AI space.

The Daily Mail ‘New Media’ (EXCLUSIVE): The Daily Mail officially launched its New Media division last week, an operation that will create upward of a dozen socially native series featuring in-house talent, according to Bob Marshall, the U.S. head of content at DMG Media. The division aims to mirror the success of its U.K. counterpart, which launched last year and has grown to over 100 staff and produces videos that average around 300,000 views apiece. The launch comes freighted with serious commercial ambitions: While social video currently represents roughly 20% of all direct advertising revenue at the Daily Mail, the company expects that figure to top 33% by 2027. The infrastructure is all there, but analyst Sheel Shah is skeptical about whether its copycat formats will prove to be a success in the long run.

Wired to the App: The Condé Nast publisher Wired launched a mobile app on Tuesday, making it the latest editorial brand to launch such a lifeboat as online traffic continues to sink. I have come to see the launching of a mobile app as a litmus test for how fervently leadership believes in a brand (as well as a reflection of the resources it has on hand to make such an investment). In an era of diminishing traffic, where only editorial titles with sticky, durable audiences will survive, media companies are having to make hard choices about which of their holdings have the highest likelihood of success. Congrats, Wired!

Ryan Merkley is the chief operating officer of NPR. He joined the company in January 2025, just months before the public media organization would face dramatic cuts to the federal funding that helps it and its nationwide network of member organizations operate.

Merkley is also intimately involved with the publisher and its artificial intelligence strategy, which involves finding innovative ways to maximize engagement in the face of declining traffic, as well as negotiating with the AI firms over licensing deals. So far, NPR has not struck any content partnerships with any of the major AI companies, although it remains in active negotiations.

This interview has been edited.

Mark Stenberg: NPR is one of the most prominent major news publishers to have neither struck a content licensing partnership with nor sued an AI firm, defying the “woo and sue” approach” I have seen used so often. Why is that?

Ryan Merkey: Blocking them is on the table, but it is more complicated for us because we are a distributed network through our member stations, so we would have to block nationwide. We are also a mission-driven organization with a mandate to serve all Americans, so access is really important to us. That being said, the integrity of answer engine results is paramount, and that has not been a top priority for many of these companies.

Mark: You have said that Google used to be incredibly rigorous about ensuring it surfaced accurate results, but that focus has disappeared in the AI era. Why do you think that is?

Ryan: It is obvious that there is urgency here, but this is the first time where a massive consumer product has arrived half-baked. The public has served as the de facto quality assurance team. It could be because of the enormous [capital expenditures] it laid out to come to market.

Mark: There is an obvious tension between your desire to remain accessible and your ability to continue operating as traffic declines. When does NPR reach an inflection point and have to do something drastic?

Ryan: Every media organization is facing that dilemma. The trend line is going down; the diminishing returns of search are pretty dramatic. We are using Piano to optimize our on-site engagement, while working to more effectively draw in audiences from popular off-platform destinations, like Tiny Desk on YouTube.

Mark: Funny enough, I spoke with Zack McCune, the director of brand at Wikimedia, about this same topic. They feel a similar tension between their mission—providing access to the world’s information—and their continued ability to operate without traffic.

Ryan: I was the chief of staff at the Wikimedia Foundation for almost three years. This is the second time they have been around the block, following Google’s launch of the Knowledge Bar. That time, Google was so careful. They had a team of engineers who scraped Wikipedia in real time but would delay information on health, finance, and living people, because they wanted to ensure that people never made a consequential decision about their lives with inaccurate information. Contrast that with the way they are behaving now, and it is night and day.

title: ESP-MQTTunnel – A $3 hardware proxy over MQTT
description: ESP32 mqtt tcp proxy - text works, otherwise slow. Contribute to hack-tramp/ESP-MQTTunnel development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
🇺🇸 English 🇨🇳 中文 🇷🇺 русский 🇮🇳 हिंदी 🇪🇸 español

A working PoC that turns an ESP32 into a $3 hardware proxy that tunnels traffic over MQTT. Because it connects out to a broker, you can bypass firewalls/censorship without open ports or public IP.

The ESP32 is the actual TCP endpoint. The Python script acts as a local proxy on the laptop. MQTT is just the pipe between them.

Tested with: Windows 10 Firefox / Python 3 <--> ESP32-S3 Dev Module <--> HiveMQ Cloud (free tier)

⚠️ The MQTT broker must be reachable from whichever country the laptop is in.

The ESP32 has limited resources and no multithreading, so it can't handle too many simultaneous connections. Trying to load pages in multiple tabs will not work.

Create a free cluster at HiveMQ Cloud (or use any MQTT broker reachable from both devices).

Edit both files and set your MQTT credentials:

Open esp.ino in the Arduino IDE, select your ESP32 board, and upload. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud to see activity. I prefer to use PuTTY so I can copy large amounts of output.

Go to Settings → General → Network Settings → Settings…

Select Manual proxy configuration

Set HTTPS Proxy to 127.0.0.1 port 8080

Make sure localhost and 127.0.0.1 are not in the "No proxy for" list

Visit any HTTPS site. Traffic will relay through MQTT to the ESP32 and out to the real server.

type is one of open, data, close

data is base64-encoded raw bytes, or null for open/close

conn_id identifies the TCP connection (Firefox opens several in parallel)

title: OMLX creator&maintainer Jun Kim joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community
description: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
fullText:
MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

title: A Self-Evident Essay Arguing for the Use of AI in Writing
description: A Self-Evident Essay Arguing for the Use of AI In Writing - Sheer-Economics/the-sins-of-AI-writing
fullText:
This little project is meant to argue for the use of AI, and to demonstrate the
use of AI in the process of forming the argument itself.
It is best to inspect the commit differences with the --word-diff flag.

The draft was written quickly, after thinking about the issue for one evening.

After the draft, I needed a plugin for the Vim editor to hook into Claude Code.
None existed off-the-shelf, so I talked to Claude and settled on using
tpope/vim-dispatch with some Claude-generated Vim functions.

It was done paragraph by paragraph.
The process was slow because I wouldn't let go of the opportunity to learn from
fixing those grammar errors.

When the first half of the essay was done, I started to rewrite the second half,
realizing it was poorly constructed.

I set out to configure the tool prettier with a plugin to enable a
one-sentence-per-line format, so that the differences between commits could be
easily inspected.

I fixed grammar errors in the second half of the essay.

Then, I felt the example in the last section might not be well received.
Despite being a genuine personal example, it could spark an unnecessary,
off-topic argument about ad promotion.
I flagged it to rewrite later.

Claude raised 12 structure issues in one run.
Of these, 9 were accepted as suggested, 2 were accepted with edits, and 1 piece
of advice was followed.

It also flagged a lack of parallelism in the section headings.
As a result, two subtitles were updated.

I replaced it with a general example, as flagged previously.

title: Londoner jailed for selling £2.7M of fake vinyl on "industrial scale"
description: He pleaded guilty to two charges
fullText:
A man has been jailed for selling £2.7million worth of fake vinyl by the likes of The Beatles, Taylor Swift and Ed Sheeran.

Rehan Ahmed from west London, was sentenced at Inner London Crown Court last Friday (September 18) in what City of London Police called “a long‑running, highly organised and entirely unlicensed manufacturing operation”.

He pleaded guilty to two charges of breach of artists’ copyright, and acquiring and using criminal property. On the first count, Judge Darren Reed sentenced him to two years and eight months in prison, while the more serious second charge led to a custodial penalty of three and a half years.

The sentences will be served concurrently, meaning that the second will dictate the time Ahmed spends in prison, according to The Guardian.

Ahmed produced counterfeit vinyl albums under the company names Phoenix of Vinyl and Paragon Music, which he supplied to record shops or sold directly to consumers through online platforms such as Discogs and eBay.

His record factory was raided in February 2024 after the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) made a test purchase from the premises and discovered evidence of counterfeiting, according to BBC News.

City of London Police said officers uncovered the largest stash of fake vinyl ever found in the UK, with 2,791 records by 108 different artists including Adele, Beyoncé and Rihanna using four 70-year-old vinyl presses over a period of seven years.

He added: “With music on physical formats enjoying a resurgence, the market in counterfeit records has unfortunately also been growing as criminals cash in at the expense of creators and fans.

“This doesn’t just impact the legal music economy and everyone that works and invests in it – it also affects every one of us as citizens who fall victim to other forms of criminality that it funds.”

The UK’s best-selling vinyl albums and singles of 2026 so far include Harry Styles‘ recent LP ‘Kiss All The Time. Disco, Occasionally’, Olivia Dean‘s ‘The Art Of Loving’ and Gorillaz‘ latest record, ‘The Mountain’.

Elsewhere, CD revenue in the US surged by nearly 60 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to The Recording Industry Association Of America’s new mid-year report.

title: Glamorgan great Ingram retires for coaching role
description: Glamorgan's South Africa batter Colin Ingram is to retire aged 41 after 11 seasons with the county and will take up a coaching role at Sophia Gardens.
fullText:
Glamorgan's South Africa batter Colin Ingram is to retire at the end of the season after 11 seasons with the county.

The 41-year-old says he will be taking on a coaching role with Glamorgan after 20 years of following his "dream of playing" and having "lived that every day".

Ingram is Glamorgan's longest-serving overseas player of the 21st century and was their top run-scorer in the Championship promotion-winning side in 2025.

He has scored 31 centuries for Glamorgan across the three formats with a career-best of 257 not out, and captained them in T20 cricket in 2018 and 2019.

Ingram made 40 international appearances in limited-overs matches for South Africa, where he represented Free State, Eastern Province and Warriors at domestic level, as well as playing part of the 2014 season for Somerset.

"Throughout my career I've dreamed big, worked hard, made memories, laughed and cried and seen things and places I never thought possible," he said.

"I've had a full crack and left it all out there."

Glamorgan's director of cricket Mark Wallace described Ingram as a "legend" of the club who has "had a lasting impact" on the county.

Bowler Morris set to leave Glamorgan

How new-look Glamorgan are preparing for pro level

The hard-hitting left-hand batter arrived at Sophia Gardens in 2015, quickly becoming a leading part of the team and a fan favourite.

He then played little Championship cricket for a five-year spell because of knee problems and T20 franchise commitments around the world.

Ingram featured in an impressive range of tournaments in Australia, India, Pakistan, the West Indies and the Middle East, as well as his native South Africa and the UK's Hundred competition, for Oval Invincibles.

Ingram, who returned to longer-form cricket in recent years after a successful knee operation, described cricket as his "art".

"I was fascinated by the game from a young age, and in particular batting," he said in a social media post announcing his retirement.

"At times, when it flows everything slows down and it feels like the most natural, instinctual thing I've ever done.

"Like my form of art and the bat my paint brush and it's exhilarating."

This season he scored centuries against Yorkshire and Warwickshire in the Championship and played a leading role in the home win over Surrey with 80 and 61 not out, but made only three limited-overs appearances.

He could return for a final farewell alongside fellow retiring stalwart Chris Cooke, 40, in the closing Championship match against Essex.

Ingram has an amazing county record of 5645 runs in first-class cricket averaging 47, plus 2630 runs at an average of 62 in one-day matches, and 3431 at 32 in T20 games.

He also took 67 wickets bowling leg-spin, mainly in limited-overs matches, and filled in as an occasional wicket-keeper.

On his future plans the South African said:

"As one chapter closes the next opens beyond the boundary as I begin my coaching career.

"My art is complete but I hope to influence the game positively and inspire players to be the best they can while enjoying their journeys."

Director of cricket Wallace said: "Colin Ingram is a Glamorgan legend. His performances, his leadership, and his character have had a lasting impact on this club.

"He has been central to our progress over the last 11 years, and his influence will continue through his new coaching role.

"We thank him for everything he has given to Glamorgan and look forward to seeing him shape the future of our playing group."

title: 'This is not Wrexham. I'm not Ryan Reynolds' - behind the scenes at world's oldest club
description: A new BBC podcast Mud, Sweat and Cheers: Trouble at the Bottom – Sheffield FC goes behind the scenes on an extraordinary season at the world's oldest football club.
fullText:
A football club at the heart of a tug-of-war between a Qatari-backed venture capital firm and a rock star probably isn't that unusual nowadays.

This is the position that Sheffield FC, founded in 1857 and widely considered the world's oldest football club, were in earlier this year.

Mud, Sweat and Cheers: Trouble at the Bottom – Sheffield FC, a six-part podcast series from BBC Local and BBC Radio Sheffield and hosted by Sheffield singer-songwriter Self Esteem, goes behind the scenes during an extraordinary season for an extraordinary club.

The Club, as they're aptly nicknamed given their historic place in the sport, helped to underpin many of the laws of the modern game with the 'Sheffield Rules' and are one of just two clubs to have been awarded Fifa's prestigious Order of Merit, alongside 15-time European Cup winners Real Madrid.

Interest in the club from Qatar isn't actually anything new, a delegation from the country visited in 2017 in the build up to hosting the 2022 World Cup.

Despite Yorkshire AI Labs, backed by money from the Middle East country, saying they had plans to build a 15,000-seat stadium and a football museum it was Jon McClure, lead singer of Sheffield indie band Reverend and the Makers, who became chairman in March.

McClure is honest and up front about the goals for a club who might be the oldest in the world but have never played in the Football League and whose best FA Cup runs were reaching the fourth round in 1879 and 1880.

"This is not Wrexham. I'm not Ryan Reynolds. Let's get it clear, I'm in an indie band. I know my place in this world," McClure told BBC Radio Sheffield in March.

"I've taken a lot of advice from football people. I'm not a football person, and I won't be involved in football stuff."

In recent years Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have helped Wrexham soar through the divisions from the National League up to the Championship.

This might not be Wrexham but McClure, who has also taken over at the club's women's side who play in the fourth tier, has plans for a football academy, eSports hub, national football festival, clothing brand, visitor centre, TV show and getting the club back playing in the city of their and the wider game's birth.

Since 2001 they have played at the Coach and Horses Ground (behind, unsurprisingly, the Coach and Horses pub) in Dronfield, North Derbyshire.

The ground's seen better days, with one female supporter telling the podcast the women's toilets are "disgusting".

"I think everybody wants the club back in the city, but there's only Sheffield that could invent football and build a B&Q car park on it," McClure says in relation to the site of their original home now being occupied by a DIY shop.

With the Club challenging to go up from the United Counties League Premier Division North at the back end of the 2025-26 campaign McClure offers free entry to under-16s to try and boost the atmosphere.

"We're pushing for promotion. Obviously, we've got this under-16s come for nowt," he says.

"They're good kids. I've said to them overnight, 'listen, lads, we need more noise out of you'.

"They were a bit quiet. So I said, 'look, if you bring a drum, I'll buy you all a pie'. So I owe them all a pie. Well, a fair trade's no robbery, is it?"

However as good as McClure's intentions might be, not everyone is delighted with the new fans.

One complains about the abuse of players and an announcement is read out over the Tannoy at one game asking them to "refrain from throwing drinks" after a supporter is drenched in lemonade.

The push for an immediate return to the eighth tier is spearheaded by striker Alex Hardwick.

Off the field, Hardwick, like the rest of his team-mates, has another job. His though is a little more unusual than others.

"I'm a design engineer here at the AMRC (advanced manufacturing research centre). I work in a design and prototyping building. I work on a range of different projects, which range from nuclear to automotive," he says.

When he isn't busy with his day job or plundering goals, Hardwick is always willing to help out if one of the lads has an issue with their car and adds that a couple of them "do not know their way around an engine".

Boss Vill Powell acknowledges Hardwick "brings a different dynamic to the dressing room, in terms of his conversation, in terms of his banter, in terms of how he is in general".

Watching on from the stands, hopefully not soaked in lemonade, his grandparents are his number one fans.

"I just love it. I enjoy it. I get disappointed when he can't get a goal," his grandma says.

"We encourage him all the time. I don't disappoint him. Marks out of 10? Yeah, I give him 9.5," his grandad adds.

McClure feels that the Club and the city itself have not done enough to celebrate their role in the history of football.

"For far too long now this city has not shouted about itself. It's enough now," he said.

"Now's our time to stand up and say this city's brilliant.

"We invented this game, and this club invented this game, and we're going to celebrate that."

It's a sentiment shared by the fans, with one saying "if the first club in the world was based in Manchester, it would be all over everywhere. If it was in London, it would be all over everywhere. We do nothing about it" while another adds "I certainly believe Sheffield Club should be held in higher esteem".

Like anyone involved in football management and administration one thing McClure wants more than anything else now is something the world's oldest football club knows all about. Time.

Upon taking over he said: "Judge it in a year. If it's not tangibly in a better place than it is now, come and see me at a match and discuss why you think that's not the case."

title: What's gone wrong at Lancashire?
description: Lancashire are set to end 2026 in the bottom two of Division Two, their lowest-ever finish in the County Championship.
fullText:
With one match of the 2026 season remaining, unwanted history beckons for Lancashire.

This proud county is staring at the lowest finish in their 136 years of competing in the Championship. They are seventh in Division Two and could finish bottom.

Never before have Lancashire ended a season either 17th or 18th position out of all the first-class counties, but after a miserable summer of red-ball cricket, it is now staring them in the face.

They begin the final round of games nine points above bottom side Gloucestershire, but it would be little surprise if Lancashire, who welcome runaway Division Two champions Durham starting on Thursday, were overtaken and ended up bottom of the pile given how the last few months have played out.

So how has it gone so wrong for one of English cricket's traditional powerhouses?

Since the launch of the two-tier system in 2000, Lancashire had previously spent only three years in Division Two, bouncing back to the top flight as champions at the first time of asking on each occasion.

But following a fourth relegation two years ago, things have been far from straightforward in the second tier.

Expecting a quick turnaround, head coach Dale Benkenstein left the club halfway through the 2025 season after Lancashire started with no wins from their opening seven Championship games.

Just before his own departure, Benkenstein had talked about a lack of clarity , externalwithin the club about whether the priority was to produce a winning team or to bring through young players. Fast forward over 12 months and that perceived issue has not been resolved.

Former player Steven Croft took over in an interim role from the South African and with three wins from the second half of the season with improved cricket and morale, he was handed the head coach job permanently.

With England legend James Anderson taking on the captaincy on a permanent basis for 2026, the hope was Lancashire would be challenging for promotion this year.

That certainly looked the case as the Red Rose won two and drew one of their first three matches, as Anderson took 21 wickets, including a match-winning 4-18 against Derbyshire.

However, a victory over Gloucestershire in Bristol was one that came at a heavy price as opener Luke Wells and new quick bowler Ajeet Singh Dale picked up injuries that turned out to be season-ending.

From that point in mid-April, the wheels have fallen off in a big way. Lancashire have proceeded to lose eight of the next 10 Championship matches, with the other two being rain-affected draws.

And it is in batting where the Red Rose's flaws have been primarily exposed.

Lancashire have posted one batting bonus point from the past nine matches - a total of 281-8 declared against Worcestershire in May - the only time a first innings score has ticked past 250.

Since the Championship resumed at the end of August, Lancashire's highest total in nine completed first and second innings is 192, with teenager Rocky Flintoff's 65 the highest individual score.

There have only been three Championship centuries all season and collapses have become commonplace, meaning the end-of-year batting averages are going to make for gruesome reading.

Take the last match against Kent. Openers Michael Jones and Jennings battled through the whole morning session on the opening day without losing a wicket, yet within 20 minutes of the restart after lunch, Lancashire had fallen from 81-0 to 82-4 and eventually lost all 10 wickets in the session to be all out for 161.

With the ball, no side has collected more bowling points than Lancashire, while Anderson and George Balderson are two of only six Division Two bowlers to take 50 wickets or more and the only ones in the same side.

But with not enough runs to play with, it has been hard to put opposition teams under serious and lasting pressure.

27 April: Durham (a) - LOST by eight wickets

10 May: Middlesex (h) - LOST by six wickets

18 May: Worcestershire (h) - Match drawn

14 June: Kent (h) - LOST by 140 runs

21 June: Derbyshire (a) - LOST by nine wickets

23 August: Northants (h) - LOST by 316 runs

30 August: Worcestershire (a) - Match drawn

4 September: Middlesex (a) - LOST by 160 runs

11 September: Gloucestershire (h) - LOST by 105 runs

17 September: Kent (a) - LOST by seven wickets

Lancashire's title success in 2011 is their only sole Championship win since 1934, but that should not hide the fact that they remain one of English cricket's biggest teams, able to call upon far superior resources to most of the other sides in county cricket and certainly those in Division Two.

That only makes the paucity of current performances worse and the mood around Emirates Old Trafford is dark.

Many of the club's members are unhappy at how they believe cricket has been secondary in recent years to concerts and conferences and more attention diverted towards Manchester Super Giants in The Hundred.

Chief executive Daniel Gidney is stepping down, with Richard Kenyon arriving from Nottinghamshire to replace him while West Indies great Clive Lloyd has become the new club president and former captain and coach Mike Watkinson has been voted on to the board - with the hope of bringing cricketing expertise to fruition.

And significant change is set to happen this winter after Lancashire announced on Monday the departure of director of cricket performance Mark Chilton, the sign that things must improve on the field, with Gidney referencing the Championship as being at the heart of the club's 'cricketing vision', external.

Remarkably, Lancashire have only won two red-ball matches in four seasons at Old Trafford and fans have watched their team be out-performed on home soil in all three disciplines by Northants and Gloucestershire recently.

Confidence in the team is low and head coach Croft knows it is a tough time for all concerned.

"You don't want to go through this as a player but usually you come out of it a better player," he told BBC Radio Lancashire after the three-day loss at Kent in the last round.

"Then you don't take it for granted when it is going well. But it's a horrible place to be in, as a team as a well as individuals, we're not really clicking.

"Four-day cricket is tough. It's a competitive division, some tricky surfaces, some of the lads have to problem-solve on the job, but that's what it's about to be a good four-day side."

Scott Read, BBC Radio Lancashire commentator

The numbers are well documented, and they don't make for pretty reading. Lancashire have not made 200 in any innings since June, their last batting point came in May and not since April have they managed to pick up more than two batting points.

Since their last win in April against Gloucestershire, they have lost eight of the following 10 Championship matches.

Lancashire have never finished bottom of the County Championship; it's a fate that they will probably avoid even though bottom club Gloucestershire have managed more wins heading into the final round of games.

It's the match against Gloucestershire in Bristol where things started to go wrong this year, season-ending injuries for Ajeet Singh Dale and Luke Wells in the same game deprived them of a new marquee signing and their opening batter.

In fact, they've used seven different opening partnerships this season, their first stand of 50 for the first wicket didn't come until September. Only two players have scored a century, Marcus Harris has done it twice with Paul Coughlin batting at eight being the other.

They've used 25 different players, it's been that kind of season.

Yes, the numbers don't make for pretty reading, at least those numbers don't. In the middle of all this is a remarkable display of endurance, fitness and sheer desire to play which has seen James Anderson miss only two red-ball games.

He's captained and carried the side all summer, ending the season with over 50 wickets. Not since 2005 has Anderson taken 50 wickets in a season for Lancashire. George Balderson has also passed 50 this year, the first time in his career he's reached that milestone.

The club continue to try to give younger players a chance - Rocky Flintoff, Arav Shetty, Joe Moores and Ben Walkden all featuring. But it's 15 years ago that Lancashire last won the title, it's over a decade since they last won major silverware.

And, since finishing second in Division One in 2022 the Red Rose have only won 11 of the following 55 Championship matches, with a relegation in 2024 and are now set for a third successive season in Division Two.

Cricket has a wonderful habit of making fools of us all, it can quickly prove us all wrong, but the trend is worrying and the fear among many members is that it may take some time to turn the fortunes of this famous old club around.

title: Olympic champion Smith to come out of retirement
description: "Crazy, scaring and exciting" - South Africa's double Olympic swimming champion Tatjana Smith reverses her retirement decision to chase a spot at the LA 2028 Games.
fullText:
Double Olympic swimming champion Tatjana Smith is coming out of retirement with the aim of competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The 29-year-old, who is South Africa's most decorated Olympian, said she was "missing the water", adding her return "feels a little crazy, a little scary and very exciting all at once".

Smith, who won 100m breaststroke gold and 200m silver at the Paris 2024 Games, to add to 200m breaststroke gold and 100m silver at Tokyo 2020, is aiming to compete over a new Olympic distance of 50m.

"It's definitely a new challenge, a new event, a new race, but also a new me," she said.

"For the first time, I am choosing swimming and I am choosing the event and I am choosing a new event, that has no history but to try and write some new history.

"LA 2028 is the goal. It is not a promise. I still have to build a race, qualify and earn my place back on those blocks."

The former 200m breaststroke world record holder initially retired from swimming after the 2024 Olympics.

title: Egan's late career resurgence back to Premier League
description: BBC Sport NI looks at Republic of Ireland centre-back's John Egan's rise back to the Premier League with Hull City and the international set-up under Heimir Hallgrimsson.
fullText:
Just 18 months ago a 31-year-old John Egan was struggling for minutes off the bench for promotion-chasing Burnley and decided to make a January switch to fellow Championship side Hull City.

Fast forward to the present day and Egan is a Premier League regular for the Tigers, who have taken everyone by surprise upon their return to the top flight.

It's been quite a turnaround for the now 33-year-old, who probably thought his last Premier League appearance had already come, when he was taken off on a stretcher with a season-ending Achilles injury when playing for Sheffield United against West Ham in September 2023.

Egan has quietly rebuilt his career after being released by the Blades, first with the Clarets before finding a home at Hull after joining in 2024.

He signed a new two-year deal earlier this month, has played five of their league games and has even forced his way back into the Republic of Ireland squad.

His late career resurgence back to the Premier League is a story of perseverance and unwavering belief despite considerable adversity.

Hallgrimsson spoke to players individually about Israel games

Coleman not included in Republic of Ireland squad

Egan made 208 appearances for Sheffield United during his six seasons with the club, winning promotion to the Premier League with them in 2019 and 2023.

He was named club captain in the summer of 2023, but would play his last game for the Blades in September that same year as an Achilles injury curtailed his Premier League return and kept him out for close to 10 months.

The defender's contract expired the following summer and the club decided not to renew the deal, leaving Egan hurt and in the lurch as he tried to battle back from that serious injury and continue his career.

He went on trial to Burnley and West Ham, with then Clarets boss Scott Parker seeing enough from the experienced centre-back to offer him a one-year deal with the club seeking a quick return to the top flight after relegation the previous season.

With Burnley then getting off to a flying start in the Championship, Egan, who was working back to full fitness, was restricted to just seven appearances and decided to swap a promotion push at Turf Moor for a relegation battle with Hull just five months later.

He signed an 18-month deal and was thrown straight in, completing his first 90 minutes in over a year, coincidentally against Burnley in a 2-0 loss in February.

The Kerry native would go on to make 10 more appearances as Hull stayed up on goal difference on the final day.

Manager Sergej Jakirovic then came in and transformed the club the following campaign, with a fully-fit Egan a key player in their success.

He played 48 times as Hull sneaked into the play-offs and then beat Middlesborough in the final to return to the Premier League for the first time since 2017.

Egan picked up where he left off last season in the top flight this term, as evidenced by his performance in the opening day 2-0 victory over Manchester United.

He made 18 clearances against the Red Devils and has since helped the Tigers keep clean sheets against Coventry and Aston Villa before they earned a point against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge and lost narrowly against Newcastle.

It's been a dream return to the top flight for Hull and Egan, who have shown they are up for the fight in the battle to stay in the league.

Egan's form at Hull helped him to earn an international recall with the Republic of Ireland in October last year, after two years without a call-up.

Previously an automatic starter, the rise of the likes of Nathan Collins, Dara O'Shea and Jake O'Brien have pushed him down the pecking order and he has played a bit-part role under Heimir Hallgrimsson.

Egan came off the bench for the closing stages of the 1-0 defeat against Portugal and was then on the bench for the subsequent wins against Armenia, Portugal and famously Hungary, which gave them a shot at the World Cup via the play-offs.

He again was an unused substitute in the heartbreaking shootout defeat against Czech Republic before winning his 38th cap by starting in a 0-0 friendly draw against North Macedonia in May.

With Hallgrimsson's preference for playing with three centre-backs, Egan has certainly staked a claim for occupying one of those slots in the Nations League opener against Kosovo given his start to the season.

His case is strengthened by the fact that captain Collins is out injured, O'Brien has been limited to three appearances for Everton and O'Shea has been playing out of position at right-back for Ipswich Town.

The other centre-back options in the squad - new call-up Liam Kitching, Jimmy Dunne and James Abankwah - are inexperienced on the international stage.

Even if he does not start in Pristina, the condensed nature of the window and with a game against Austria sandwiched between two against Israel in 12 days, he is sure to see some game time for his country.

Given what he has gone through just to make it back to the top flight and into the Irish squad, Egan will fancy his chances of re-establishing himself as a starter for country as he did at club level.

title: McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years
description: Three years ago, Josh McPake was without a club. Twenty months ago, he was in the shop window but "no-one wanted him". This week, he's involved in his first Scotland camp. Here, BBC Sport Scotland charts the fall and rise of the winger who's got everyone in the country talking.
fullText:
Three years ago, Josh McPake was without a club. Twenty months ago, he was in the shop window but "no-one wanted him".

This week, he's involved in his first Scotland camp following a heroic start to life at Hearts, where, to the tune of Abba's Dancing Queen, the supporters sing he is "having the time of his life".

His call-up to Sebastien Poconogli's squad for the upcoming Nations League games caps an eventful few years for the 25-year-old winger.

From Rangers academy's next big thing, to dropping into Scottish League 1 with Stirling Albion, to being shelved at St Johnstone, it's been a colourful - and at times chaotic - career so far.

But, "I wouldn't change my journey for anything," McPake insists.

He now appears at home in Gorgie and many have hopes he will be just as comfortable when he gets the opportunity to represent his country.

His story is one of resilience and patience. And it's paying off.

BBC Sport Scotland charts the fall and rise of McPake as "he can pass, he can score, having the time of his life, Josh McPake, watch him play on a Saturday".

Sesko among three injury absences for Slovenia against Scotland

Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out

How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut?

Pocognoli Facetime helps Miller over summer of discontent

His story starts like many others, in the Ibrox academy from a young age, where he was awarded player of the year in 2019 by working up through the reserves to the fringes of the first team.

A matter of months after collecting the gong, he was given his first - and only - run-out for Steven Gerrard's side.

His appearance off the bench in Rangers' rout against Gibraltar's St Joseph's in Europa League qualifying was not a sign of things to come, as he was sent out on his first of six loan moves just one month later.

Dundee, Greenock Morton, Harrogate Town, Morecambe, Tranmere Rovers and Queen's Park all had a taste of McPake but nothing permanent was made.

He swiftly became a bit of a football nomad.

While on Tayside, he scored the winner for Scotland Under-19s against Germany, but still he was flung from pillar to post.

On 1 September 2023, he left Rangers and, though he trained with a number of clubs - where he endured some "knocks and setbacks" - he didn't find a home for another near-six months, until Stirling signed him on a short-term deal.

A dunt down to earth, no doubt, but McPake didn't allow any ego to get in his way, as then-Binos boss Darren Young recalled.

"He came into training and he was brilliant - he couldn't have done any more," former Aberdeen midfielder Young told BBC Scotland.

"He worked very, very hard. He helped put balls away after training, he was always doing extra bits of shooting and finishing - I joked to him once or twice, 'if you don't get your finger out then you'll end up back here part-time' but it was one of those where you could see his ability, he was head and shoulders above the guys.

"It was just a case of him then doing it and getting into the kind of situation where a club - and the right club - would come and get him."

He scored on his debut for the League 1 side - though that was little surprise to Young who was left "wondering why he had not been signed up" when he got the move in motion.

"We had an eye on him as he was free but it looked like he was going to sign at a higher level but another player got injured and then the move wasn't going to happen," he explained.

"He sort of found himself in limbo but I think there's a lot of positives that can be learned from that.

"He kind of said, 'well, I don't want to be in this position and I don't want to be back down there again' and the only way to do that is by working hard and working on weaknesses, which he did."

It'll be of no surprise McPake didn't lack anything in the attacking sense. A wee bit of fine tuning on his tracking back was all that was required during his time at Forthbank to fire him back to where he wanted to be.

"I didn't need to tell him how to go by a player and put it in the top corner - he had all that," Young said.

"I was just trying to say if he could fit into the structure here, work as hard at going back as he did forward, then he'd get, hopefully, an opportunity to kick on again.

"Some players don't, some players kind of have that attitude of, 'I can do it going forward, I don't need to do it going back,' but the penny dropped and he realised to improve and progress, that's what he had to add.

"He worked hard for it and he's got what he deserved."

The reward for knuckling down - and dropping down - was a move back to the top flight with St Johnstone - despite suffering relegation with Stirling Albion.

A two-year deal was agreed but he failed to force his way into Craig Levein's team, and had similar struggles when Simo Valakari took over in October 2024.

His mettle was being pushed to the max yet again.

The Finn revealed last year, external that McPake was made available in the winter transfer window while Saints were fighting for their Premiership life, but they "couldn't find him any clubs".

"We made Josh available in January and offered him to many clubs because he needed to play," Valakari said.

"The truth is, nobody wanted him. We couldn't find him any clubs.

"And, for me, that was the wake-up call for Josh. That was when he decided things had to change.

"If things had stayed the way they were then football was done for him. He would have had to go and get a normal life."

What followed was far from normal.

McPake started his first Premiership game for St Johnstone in the first of their five post-split games and kept his place until the end of the season as he registered three assists.

Saints were ultimately relegated but it set him up for the season of his dreams.

He set the tone for the Championship campaign he dominated with a hat-trick on the opening weekend against title rivals Partick Thistle.

In the second tier, his blistering pace, immense physicality and dancing feet were flung back into the spotlight. His eye for a goal - 16 all told in the division - was evident, too.

Such qualities caught the attention of then Premiership leaders Hearts, who agreed a pre-contract back in January.

But there was no head-turn from the winger, who remained fully focused on repaying the club who resurrected his career by ensuring they would be an opponent of his this season.

He ended the campaign with the mantelpiece packed with trophies and, while the personal accolades were appreciated, it was all about the Championship winners' medal for Tynecastle-bound McPake.

Ensuring adversity remained an ever present in his tale, the footballing gods - seemingly - threw another curveball McPake's way.

Though Derek McInnes was in charge when he agreed the move, the head coach had headed for Rangers by the time he got going in Gorgie.

But, despite sitting out the Champions League qualifiers against Sturm Graz and the first league game of the season under Wouter Vrancken, the Belgian has quickly found out why Hearts snapped up the Saints showman when they did.

With eight goal involvements in 11 games - his best contribution a goal and assist in the Edinburgh derby - he has made the step back up to the Premiership a seamless one and, as such, made it nigh impossible for Pocognoli to leave him out of his plans.

"I've loved every part of the journey," McPake said after answering his country's call.

"Personally, I feel I needed those experiences to become the player I am now.

"There were a lot of setbacks but going down the levels, proving myself and working my way back up taught me a lot.

"If you want something enough and work hard for it, you can achieve it.

"I don't want to stop here. I feel I've still got more to give and I'll continue working hard to show what I can do."

title: 'I'm an idiot' - Strickland survives crash with no helmet
description: UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland says he is "OK" but "an idiot" after surviving a crash in an off-road vehicle while not wearing a helmet.
fullText:
UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland says he is "OK" but "an idiot" after surviving a crash in an off-road vehicle while not wearing a helmet.

In a series of posts on Instagram, Strickland describes the crash as happening at 60mph with the vehicle rolling "around six times".

The 35-year-old American says he was a passenger in the vehicle alongside his friend Chris Cornell, who was driving.

Strickland says Cornell was taken to hospital after falling unconscious, before later posting a picture of him with his thumbs up in a hospital bed alongside an X-ray of a broken bone.

Strickland did not confirm if he went to hospital.

In footage posted after the crash, Strickland shows grazes on his head and back, before describing himself as an "idiot" for not wearing a helmet.

"Guys I'm in a real bad place. I let my buddy drive, he rolled us going like 60 (mph), we rolled like six times," said Strickland.

"That's from my head smacking the ground going 60. I didn't have a helmet on, I'm an idiot."

Strickland, who lives in Las Vegas, did not say where the crash took place, but a video posted shortly before the accident shows the UFC fighter in the desert before he went riding.

Strickland later posted an update, saying he is "a little concussed but good and wants to spar tomorrow".

"Think I'm OK, Chris is in the hospital but I think he's going to be alright," he added.

"It was the most fun I've had in a long time. My shoulder's a little sore."

Strickland is a polarising figure in MMA and has made homophobic and racist remarks as well as derogatory comments about women.

He became a two-time UFC middleweight champion by beating Khamzat Chimaev in May.

title: Red Bull's Hadjar to return at Azerbaijan Grand Prix
description: Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return at this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.
fullText:
Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return at this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

The 21-year-old Frenchman was replaced by New Zealand's Liam Lawson for races in the Netherlands, Monza and Madrid after injuring his wrist while boxing.

In statement, Red Bull said Hadjar has made a "full recovery" and will replace Lawson for the Grand Prix in Baku, which runs from 24-26 September.

"The team would like to sincerely thank Liam for his professionalism, dedication and hard work over the past three races," Red Bull added.

"Stepping in under challenging circumstances, he delivered some impressive performances and made a valuable contribution to the team."

Lawson, 24, finished seventh in Zandvoort and sixth in Madrid but failed to score a point at Monza after coming 14th.

After being replaced by Hadjar, Lawson will return to Red Bull's junior team Racing Bulls.

Hadjar, who will return to action alongside four-time world champion Max Verstappen, is eighth in the drivers' standings having scored 71 points this season.
